en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who was a bearer of the burden of the tradition of the venerable teacher Prabhākara.
The introduction to the *Vākyārthamātṛkā* together with its commentary, adorned by the commentary titled *Nyāyasiddhi* and by the notes on difficult passages (*viṣamasthala-ṭippaṇī*).
First Chapter:
Although this profound and extensive meaning has been composed in concise language, those who do not understand it in its entirety are here favored by me through compassion. (1)

In that regard, only those who maintain that the sentence-meaning is an action (kārya) assert that the meaning of the sentence consists of the being (bhāva), the productive operation (bhāvanā), and the unprecedented force (apūrva).
In this regard, it must be established that the sentence-meaning is indeed something unprecedented (*apūrva*).
Its basis is the theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) by words; therefore, he first clarifies that very point.
1072. Here, those who maintain that the sentence alone—whose division into words has completely vanished—is the signifier of the sentence-meaning;
and those who maintain that it is only the final phoneme of the sentence [that signifies it].
And as for the claim that word-meanings, even when denoted independently of one another by their respective words, bring about an understanding of their own mutual connection—
this is rejected by the following declaration: "The cognition of the sentence-meaning arises from the words alone, just as..."
In this manner, we shall set forth the doctrine of the teacher Prabhākara. // 1 //
[The meaning is derived] from the words themselves, not from the sentence, nor even from the final phoneme.
Nor does it arise from the objects themselves; such is the meaning. // 1 //

He begins to explain that point: "If the word-meanings themselves—whose capacities are exhausted solely by conveying their own meanings as related [to one another]—are understood, then the sentence-meaning is also understood in that same way. (2)

For, since words are not the means for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, it is by the impossibility of that [comprehension] otherwise that a single sentence is postulated as the means for it;
even though meaning is not understood from a word independently of its [conventional] usage.
And although it is impossible to acquire proficiency [in language] because of the infinity of sentences and their meanings, and because the Vedic meaning has no other means of access;

Nevertheless, it is maintained that one understands the meaning of a sentence from a sentence that has been refined by the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) regarding words and word-meanings, even though these are conceptual constructs. This is because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the reality of words and word-meanings as conceptual entities; for a single phoneme, when uttered, does not convey a meaning, and it is impossible to hear phonemes uttered in succession simultaneously.

The position is accepted that the final phoneme, accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme, is the conveyor of meaning; and for this, the conventional understanding of words and word-meanings at the ultimate level (*pāramārthika*) acts as a cooperative cause.

Alternatively, it is maintained that words whose meanings have been easily learned convey their own respective meanings—even though they are unconnected—to bring about the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

But if it can be established that words themselves denote their own meanings as already connected, then, because the meaning of the sentence has been understood, these [other] hypotheses find no footing. // 2 //
But how, then, is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning established if words only convey their own meanings as already connected? To this, he says:
"3. The wise declare that the very word-meanings, having attained mutual connection through the relationship of primary and subordinate, are themselves the sentence-meanings."
Now, one might object that because those [individual word-meanings] are numerous, there would likewise be numerous sentence-meanings and numerous sentences; to this he says:
"Even though the individual meanings of the words are numerous, they remain distinct from one another."
However, because they serve a single purpose, they are declared to constitute the meaning of a single sentence. // 4 //
Because they have a single effect based on that [connection], a sentence is also said to be one.
To the question, "How, then, is there a single purpose?", he says: "For the comprehension of the subordinate elements has as its sole purpose the principal element. (5)
For the purpose of making it understood how that which is the primary element is indeed distinguished, there is the presentation of the subordinate qualities;
therefore, the intended meaning (tātparya) lies in that [primary element] alone.
That alone is the object of cognition (*prameya*),
because the validity of a word is accepted only with respect to its intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*); and the comprehension of such an object does not depend upon a single word.
In that case, the sentence alone is the means of valid cognition.

For this very reason, it has been said: "In the first section of the sixth chapter, there is no such thing as a word within a sentence, nor are there any such things as word-meanings within the meaning of a sentence" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Commentary 6.1.1).
There is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for a word that exists as a separate entity;
and since word-meanings exist as separate entities, they do not constitute objects of cognition— this is the meaning.
And this has been clearly stated in that very same place [at verse 5.1076].

Now, in order to refute those who assert that the sentence alone is the expressive unit of the sentence-meaning, as well as those who maintain that it is only the final phoneme of the sentence, he says:
In linguistic usages that arise from hearing the speech of elders,
the determination of the expressive power (śakti) of words occurs through the distinction between insertion (āvāpa) and extraction (uddhāra).
Although all derivation of word meanings is preceded by the linguistic usage of elders,
and that usage occurs solely through sentences, nevertheless, when a certain word is inserted, there is the insertion of a certain meaning.
When a word is extracted [from a compound], it is understood that the expressive power of that word resides in that very same meaning;
and this being so, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is not rendered untenable.
Because the reasoning will be stated later:
by what force of an effect (*kāryabala*) could one sentence be postulated through the denial of the distinctions between the phonemes and words actually perceived in direct experience?
Furthermore: "Child, bring the cow; child..."
"Bind the cow, child! Bring the cow, child!
Bind the cow, boy!"
"Bring the cow, child!
"Bind the cow, boy! "Bring the cow, boy!"
For one who maintains that the sentence is the unit of meaning, eight expressive powers must be postulated for the eight sentences, such as "Tie up the cow.
However, for the proponent of the word (padavādin), there are only seven powers for the seven words; thus, there is parsimony in the postulation [of powers].
In this very same manner, when considering the term "white" (*śukla*), eight further [alternatives] should be postulated for those who maintain that the sentence is the expressive unit;

furthermore, it must be considered what kind of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) based upon a division of words and word-meanings—which is not ultimately real—can serve as a means [to understanding].
As for those, however, who assert that the final phoneme of the sentence is the expressive unit...
Even according to that view, since the division of word-meanings is ultimately real, the acquisition of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) is indeed possible.
Now, it is said that the acquisition of linguistic competency is precisely the grasping of the relationship between the signified and the signifier;
however, for those who maintain that the final phoneme of a sentence is the signifier, the word (*pada*) is not the signifier of the word-meaning (*padārtha*).
Therefore, even in his view, linguistic acquisition would be devoid of an object.
It is replied: it is not devoid of an object.
Because the relationship between the sign (nimitta) and the signified (naimittika) is accepted [by you], one might ask: "What is this status of being a sign for that which is non-expressive?
This is not a fault.

For when a certain word is employed in a sentence, that word serves as the cause for the cognition of the sentence-meaning as connected with the meaning of that word, even though it is not the direct denoter of that specific meaning.
However, even in his view, the burden of postulating a power (śakti) is exactly equal [to ours] according to the reasoning previously stated.

As for those who claim that it is the sentence itself, as it ascends into memory, that conveys the meaning of the sentence—for them too, the previously mentioned objection characterized by the excessive burden of postulating a new power (*śakti*) remains unavoidable.

Furthermore, the statement of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), "The final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, is the conveyor [of the meaning]" (*Śābarabhāṣya*, p. 46), would be rendered devoid of subject matter.
Furthermore, it is impossible to remember a great sentence (mahāvākya) all at once;
therefore, one must rely on the expressive power residing in the words themselves.
On this point, some raise an objection: "But surely, in a sentence employed in the linguistic usage of elders, it is not even possible to determine the expressive power of the words."
This is because a human statement is accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its object by virtue of being a logical mark (*liṅga*).
For, from the sentence—which is the effect—one infers the speaker’s prior cognition regarding that object, which serves as the cause.
And since that cognition is non-deviant with respect to the object of knowledge, there arises a certainty regarding the object itself, which is the thing to be known.
Nor is there an apprehension of the expressive power [of words].
It is said in reply:
Surely you do not correctly comprehend the meaning set forth in the path of logic.

For this has already been addressed there: a child, while being trained, understands that the comprehension of meaning—which is inferred from the specific activity occurring immediately after the elder (the *prayojyavṛddha*) hears a word—is caused by that word.
Having thus become proficient, he sometimes encounters a sentence composed of words whose meanings are not mutually connected.

Upon encountering such a thing, a reflection arises in him: "How could this sentence, which contains a composition of words with potentially unconnected meanings, have produced a certain cognition of meaning for the elder?"

Even for an elderly man, since his speech depends upon human agency, the suspicion that he might have composed words whose meanings are not syntactically connected is possible for me just as it was for him;
when such doubt arises, the following certainty then occurs to him:
"Surely this speaker has determined this [meaning] beforehand, thinking that he would employ only those words whose meanings are mutually connected."

Furthermore, such a restriction regarding the employment of words would not be possible if a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) were unperceived; thus, by inferring the perception of a positive concomitance, the concomitance is ascertained.
Once the concomitance is ascertained, this sentence becomes a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that meaning.
And if, by virtue of being a restatement, that sentence is indeed expressive of that meaning, [then the sentence is valid].
It is held that the cognition of the speaker's capacity to denote [the object] as previously [perceived] is not erroneous;
at most, it was simply not understood by me before that his determination of the object was preceded by inference.
Furthermore, this inference of the specific speaker’s cognition occurs when the relation [of the word] to the object has not yet been determined.
That [cognition] also does not arise from the mere comprehension of the individual forms of the words,
but rather from the comprehension of their specific [meaning]; and no specific meaning of the words is understood other than their capacity (śakti).
Therefore, just as I have done, this person has also ascertained the denotative power of words;
thus, by employing words that denote a specific relation, he has inferred the speaker’s prior cognition regarding that object—
how profound is this great ocean of logic!
The suspicion that the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of related meanings) is untenable:
On this point, some say—“Let it be granted that there is knowledge of the word-potencies (*śakti*) regarding word-meanings; nevertheless, the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* is not established.”

For instance: because the counter-correlates (pratiyogins) are infinite, the positive concomitants (anvayas) are infinite; and since those concomitants are infinite, the related items (anvitās) are also infinite, making it difficult to grasp the relationship.
Furthermore, if a word whose relationship has not been grasped were to possess denotative power (vācakatva), [it would lead to absurdity].
Furthermore, the claim that there is a denotation of a general concomitance (*sāmānyānvaya*) is not even to be considered,
because from sentences one understands a specific concomitance (*viśeṣānvaya*).

Moreover, since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is achieved even by the denotation of the mere individual forms (*svarūpamātra*), resorting to the theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) involves the fault of postulating an excessive burden of expressive power (*śaktikalpanā-gaurava*).

Likewise, when a word's own meaning is expressed as being connected with [another], one must consider the following alternative: is it expressed as being connected with another word-meaning that has already been expressed,
or with one that has not been expressed?
If it were by what is not expressed,
there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of all [meanings] from a single [word];
if it were by what is expressed, [the same fault follows].
In that case as well, since a word expresses its meaning by denoting what is connected [with others], it would require the meaning conveyed by other words for its own expression;
thus, a circular dependency (itaretarāśraya) results.
Therefore, words perform the expression of meanings solely through their own intrinsic form, without depending on the expression provided by other words.
And those word-meanings, being thus expressed by words and possessing expectancy, proximity, and compatibility, bring about the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.
It should not be suspected that they depend upon the apprehension of a relation [between themselves],
for this is a property of the words themselves.
This is not the nature of the meaning;
thus the author of the Bhāṣya says: "For words, having denoted their respective meanings, cease their operation."
"Now, having themselves been understood, they cause the meaning of the sentence to be understood" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā 1.1.25). // 6 //
He begins to refute this [view]:
"Words are deposited and extracted with their own meanings which possess syntactic connection;
therefore, the capacity of words is understood to reside only in those [meanings] that are already connected. (7)

In that very context, a doubt is raised according to the view of the Vārttika: Here it is said—Granted that insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*uddhāra*) have as their objects only the word-meanings as already connected; nevertheless, the denotation of the connected meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) remains impossible.

For that [causality] is established even through a traditional succession (pāramparya). To explain: although a meaning expressed by words is not itself syntactically connected, it becomes the cause for the comprehension of a connected meaning; thus, words possess causality with respect to the connected meanings through a traditional succession.
Regarding this, the venerable authors of the Vārttika say:
"For us, words do not relinquish their capacity even with respect to the sentence-meaning; that [sentence-meaning] is understood from the word-meanings once these have been concluded in themselves."
[Ślokavārttika, Adhikaraṇa 7, Śloka 229].
Furthermore, the presentation of the meanings of individual words is the intermediate operation of those words employed for the sake of comprehending the meaning of the sentence;
this indeed is their conventional usage.
"In their activity toward the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, the presentation of word-meanings is an inseparable concomitant, just as fire is for wood in the process of cooking. (1097)
[Ślokavārttika, Adhikaraṇa 7, Śloka 343].
Having set aside this objection for now, he refutes another defect:
"Those [words] which are connected with other meanings that are obtained through expectancy, proximity, and compatibility..."
When one relies upon the etymological derivation that words denote their own meanings (svārtha), [then... // 8 //
At that time, there is no fault whatsoever due to infinity and deviation.

As for what was stated— that because of infinity, the determination of the word’s expressive power is impossible, and that if something were expressive when its power had not been grasped, it would result in the fallacy of deviation— [that is not a fault].
That is untenable;
for even by resorting to an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), the understanding of the relation [between word and meaning] occurs,

and the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) is adopted that a word expresses its own meaning as connected with what is required, what is semantically suitable, and what is proximate, due to the ease [of such comprehension].
Therefore—
whatever is required and is suitable, when it attains proximity,
the word conveys its own meaning as qualified by that [meaning].
This is the summary verse.
Regarding the object of inquiry, there is the presentation and refutation of the Nyāya view. But what, then, is this "inquiry" (ākāṅkṣā)?
The desire to know on the part of the seeker: what, then, is its cause? Some say it is caused by invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
For action is inseparable from its factors;
thus, having perceived the action, one desires to know the factor, and likewise, having understood the factor, one [desires to know] the action.
We consider that to be incorrect, because the cessation of inquiry would be untenable. To explain:
first, when there is inquiry regarding the causal factors (*kāraka*),...

At that time, there would also arise a desire to know his progenitor, his qualities, his actions, his other causal factors (*kāraka*), and so forth. Now, if it is argued that nothing other than the causal factors is sought after because of a lack of purpose,
then even when only the action (*kriyā*) is understood, there will be cases where there is no purpose for knowing the causal factors.
In that case, there would be no desire to know [the agent],
because once an action is understood as something to be performed, it is impossible to carry it out without its factors (kārakas); therefore,
knowledge of the factor [of agency] would have no purpose.

However, in cases such as the statement of a present fact (*vartamānāpadeśa*), since it is not something to be performed, there is no purpose for knowledge of the factors of action (*kāraka*). Nevertheless, even where a sentence is considered incomplete, its incompleteness consists in its expressing a meaning that requires further supplementation (*sākāṅkṣa*).
For this very reason, they even supply ellipses there;
and even in cases where the action to be performed is understood, there would still be a desire to know all the factors of action (kārakas) in their entirety.
For example, in the case of [the command] "Devadatta,
bring the cow," there would be incompleteness due to the non-employment of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
However, since the performance [of the action] is possible even through the cognition of a single factor (*kāraka*), there is no desire to know other factors.
In that case, Devadatta,
even when the word "staff" is employed in the command, "Bring the cow with a staff," there would be no expectancy for it.
And consequently, because that [word "staff"] is not required, its connection would not occur within the meaning of the sentence.
If it is argued that a requirement for it is postulated there due to the utterance of the word "staff," [we reply:]...
Otherwise, if the referent of the word *daṇḍa* (staff) were not syntactically connected, the utterance of that word would be purposeless.

Similarly, in the case of the passage, "He buys Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, yellow-eyed [cow]" (*aruṇayā ekahāyanyā piṅgākṣyā somaṃ krīṇāti*), there would likewise be the consequence of a lack of syntactic connection.
For there is no authority whatsoever to suggest that the utterance of a Vedic word must not be purposeless.

Therefore, there is no cause for the arising of an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in that regard; consequently, anything additional [to the word] "he buys soma" would lack syntactic connection (*ananvitatā*).
Moreover, because the action and its factors are worldly (*laukika*), [they do not require a Vedic injunction].
Since the accomplishment of that [object] is not obstructed even when some action and its factors are undertaken, a desire to know the specific details does not arise excessively;
for a desire for knowledge occurs regarding what is unknown,
but not regarding what is already known.
The statement of expectancy according to his own view:
the non-termination of the denotation is the basis for the arising of the desire to know.
For when a single word is employed—such as "door" (*dvāra*) and so forth—the denotative function itself does not reach completion.
For as long as the word that brings the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) into proximity has not been uttered, it is impossible to speak of "denotation of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*).
Since it has been established— by virtue of the linguistic usage of elders— that words have as their purpose the communication of a meaning already related [to others],
the desire to know that counter-correlative is indeed appropriate for that purpose.

Even for one whose established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that "the connection [of meaning] is expressed" (*abhihitānvaya*), since in that view a word-meaning lacks the capacity for connection without another word-meaning,
the desire to know the counter-correlate (*pratiyogijijñāsā*) is indeed appropriate for the sake of establishing that [connection].
And since that [incompleteness] exists, and because it is well known in the world that ellipses are supplied to complete an unfinished sentence,
an appropriate correlate is supplied by virtue of the context and other factors.

This is so even in cases such as "On the new moon day, in the afternoon, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña," where, despite the use of multiple words, there is still the expression of a related meaning through the process of *anvitābhidhāna*.
For that which is stated as an effect, being of a nature not previously existent, its status as an effect is untenable without its performance;
that performance is impossible without an agent;
and that [agency] is incompatible without a qualification to act (*adhikāra*).
Since that [injunction] cannot be conceived without a person to be enjoined,
it is indeed appropriate to desire to know an enjoinable agent capable of being connected with it; for when such a desire exists,
one perceives its incompleteness.

Even though, as in common worldly practice, one might supply an ellipsis, since the necessity of life is both internal and essential, it cannot be assumed that the injunction implies its performance; therefore, setting that aside, when the qualification of the person entitled to act (*niyojya-viśeṣaṇa*) is established as being optional (*kāmya*), heaven alone— pervading all persons desiring objects— is fit to serve as the qualification of the person entitled to act.

In the case [of the injunction to sacrifice], one who desires heaven is supplied as the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). However, in the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), since the purpose to be accomplished is already fulfilled by the performance prompted by another [injunction], no person to be enjoined is supplied.
Furthermore, because the "newly-acquired" (*apūrva*) result is something transcendent (*alaukika*), the expectancy regarding the person to be enjoined is not satisfied without such a supply.

And precisely because it is non-worldly (*alaukika*), in such cases as "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya with white rice in clarified butter" (*Mai. Saṃ. 2.2.2*), since the injunction cannot be established without an understanding of the assistance rendered by the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*), there arises the desire to know that [assistance], and consequently, the desire to know the categories of meaning that produce it.
For this very reason, in the absence of that [expectancy], the author of the Bhāṣya, suspecting a deficiency in the sentences, offered a rebuttal:
"But if that is so, then three words are employed there in common usage—'Bring the white cow' (gām ānaya śuklām).
Since two factors of action (kārakas) are impossible there, there is no expectancy; how then can there be the expression of the related meaning (anvitābhidhāna)?"
“Because the sentence is complete with just ‘Bring the cow’—
true,
this is so provided that no other words are uttered.”
But once that [word] has been uttered,
because it is understood as a single syntactical unit with the word "brings" (*ānayati*) due to its proximity, it denotes its own meaning as connected with the act of bringing;
and since that is impossible without a mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
Expectancy is postulated for the verbal root *ā-nī* (to bring).
And so it has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "And there is expectancy toward 'red'. [Śābarabhāṣya, p. 117]
Therefore, here too, expectancy exists precisely for the sake of establishing the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related). At most, this is the distinction:
in cases such as "The door," expectancy belongs to that very word itself for the purpose of expressing what is related.
But in cases such as "Bring the white cow," [the requirement] belongs to another word.
That inquiry regarding a correlate (pratiyogin), which serves either to express a related meaning or to connect the stated meanings,
is proclaimed as "expectancy" (ākāṅkṣā).
Thus is the summary verse.
And this very expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), being present, is relied upon as the defining characteristic for linguistic proficiency. Why, then, is mere proximity and semantic competency not relied upon?
Because we do not observe the expression of a related meaning in the case of those words that lack expectancy.
In such cases as “This son of the king comes; let this man be removed,” the king—who has no expectancy for a connection with the word "son"—is not construed with the "man.

But why is it that, despite there being no difference between these two—the son and the man—in terms of proximity (*sannidhi*) and semantic fitness (*yogyatva*), the king is connected only with the son?
It is not [understood] by the person alone.
It is said: because the comprehension of the sentence-meaning from a sentence depends upon reasoning (*nyāya*), the king is connected only with a son who is inherently dependent [upon him].

And since that which has no expectancy for connection with anything else does not undergo a connection with a person, expectancy is also accepted as a defining characteristic of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*).
For even if something is fit and proximate, there is no syntactic integration (*anvaya*) unless it is complete;
therefore, in the context of linguistic competency, expectancy is likewise a defining characteristic of words.
Thus is the summary verse.
Furthermore, this expectancy does not arise all at once toward all possible counter-correlates,
but rather according to the sequence of the occurrence of its causes.
For instance, it is impossible to even conceive of a novel effect without an object [to produce it].
First, there is an expectation regarding the object which constitutes the accompaniment of the performance of the injunction.

Then, once the meaning of the injunction— consisting of the connection with the object— is understood, there arises an expectation for a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), because its fulfillment is impossible without such a person.
Thus, when the objective meaning has become the object [of cognition] and the instrument is obtained,
there arises in the apūrvas of the modified rites a requirement for the assistance of the instrument;
and once that [assistance] is obtained, [the requirement is satisfied].
"Thus, there is an expectancy for the objects that produce it.
And so they have said:
"Among all counter-correlatives, no expectancy arises at that very moment."
But according to the sequence of the occurrence of causes, each in its proper order.
Thus it is said.
Accordingly, even the denotation of the related [words] occurs precisely in that sequence.
And there is a verse on this point:
"In whatever manner the desire to know arises in the listener regarding the related [objects],"
In that very same way, words denote their meanings as already connected.
The Definition of Proximity (*Sannidhi*). Now, what is proximity?
It is the mental representation of another meaning that occurs immediately after hearing a given word, by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and semantic compatibility (*yogyatā*).

And that [capacity for denoting the related] is not based on words alone; it is merely an indicator in the acquisition of the knowledge of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related), because in common usage, *anvitābhidhāna* is observed even when [a word] is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*).
Nor should it be said that "it is the word itself that is supplied, and that word brings the meaning to mind."
Because it serves no purpose and because it lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even if the *adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis) were based on the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), [it would still be untenable].
Nevertheless, the postulation of a word is untenable;
for that very thing without which there would be an inconsistency is the object of knowledge through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Nor is there an impossibility of objects existing without words.

It might be argued that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) proceeds precisely for the sake of postulating an object, because that object is cognizable through conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*).
And because determinate cognitions are preceded by words, it follows that they terminate in the word itself as being present before one—
this is incorrect;
for even though determinate cognition is preceded by a word, [the object] remains the inferential mark (liṅga).
Furthermore, since the sense organs possess their power determined toward the object itself during the state of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpaka*), they do not terminate in the mere word;

likewise, in the case of presumption based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*), it is accepted that the validity of the presumption resides in the object itself which directly accounts for the perceived fact;
similarly, even in the case of presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*), it is logical that its validity lies in that very [object], not in the word.
This is because it is incapable of directly pacifying [the opponent's] objection.
Furthermore, in every conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), the word that revolves in memory cannot itself be established as the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Moreover, the fact that a word was previously perceived in conceptual cognitions is not at all authoritative as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavatī*).
However, it is established by experience that the recollection of the word occurs at the very same time as the comprehension of the meaning;
therefore, verbal presumption (*śrutārthāpatti*) does not have the word as its object. Nor is it appropriate to postulate a word solely on the grounds of the word's own inconsistency.
Since there is no impossibility regarding its own [meaning],
the conceptual construction proceeding from the impossibility of denoting a related [meaning] remains restricted to objects that are suitable correlates,
because only those are required.
By the principle of the tenth [chapter] and so forth, even though the word was previously perceived, it must be disregarded just like the meaning of the word (*padārtha*).
Nor is it the case that where there is an ellipsis such as "the door," one should supply [the verb] "let it be opened" (*āvriyatām*) there as well.
Or rather, the capacity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) to conceive [the word] as "let it be supplied" arises because it is merely the cause for the postulation of a general [word];
therefore, since it completes what is incomplete, the supply of an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is established even from the perspective of common worldly usage.
In that case, because the specific meaning is determined through suitability and by virtue of the context and so forth, and because it is the meaning alone that completes the sense,
the supply of a word [not present in the text] is useless.
Therefore, in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, it is established through the person to be enjoined; everywhere, through the assistance of the instrument;

and in the case of modified sacrifices (vikṛtis), even through the archetypal elements (prākṛta-padārthas) which are not explicitly presented by the words—thus, the theory of "denotation of the related" (anvitābhidhāna) is proven.

Just as there is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), so too, even when proximity (*sannidhi*) is present, the sequence [of words] must be understood according to the order of the factors that bring about that proximity;

and accordingly, the denotation of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) occurs in that very same way. Furthermore, in the process of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*), proximity arising from the word itself is not the defining characteristic.
For in the world, a relationship is observed even with a meaning that has been supplied by ellipsis.
The proximity of all counter-correlates does not occur simultaneously;
rather, it occurs sequentially according to the sequence of the causal complex that brings them into proximity.
In whatever manner the proximity of counter-correlates arises,
in that very same manner, through words, there occurs a sequential comprehension of the related meaning.
These are the summary verses. Therefore,

the meaning is that it is connected with another word-meaning which has been obtained through expectancy, proximity, and compatibility, as previously described— namely, that which is expected, proximate, and suitable.
The Determination of Fitness.
What is this so-called "fitness"?
It is said: that which is worthy of connection.
How is it understood that "this [word] is capable of being related"?
Because it is observed as being related. [Objection:
If that is so, then how can there be an expression of the relation (anvitābhidhāna) with the unprecedented (apūrva) task in the Veda?

Because no relation whatsoever is observed with that [unseen factor], it is said: there is no fault, for the determination of general capacity (*yogyatā*) is the means for the cognition of the particular (*viśeṣa*). As for that which is unprecedented (*apūrva*),...
That too is indeed an effect; whatever has an observed relationship with an effect is determined to be "capable" (yogya).
It is precisely as a generality that capability is established in the world.
This serves as an indicative mark for the acquisition of the linguistic convention regarding the denotation of that which is associated with it.
This is the summary verse.
[Now follows] the presentation and refutation of other views regarding the subject of fitness (*yogyatā*). Others, however, hold that what has not been determined as unfit is fit.
They say that even by means of this non-worldly (alaukika) meaning of the injunction, the theory of "denotation of the related" (anvitābhidhāna) is established;
however, this is without substance.
For it is impossible for anyone to determine the competency (yogyatā) regarding an entity that is not cognizable through other means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).
In the same way, even regarding incapacity (*ayogyatā*), there would be a logical connection (*anvaya*) with it in every respect, even though it is not perceived by everyone.
For the connection occurs only with the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) as the object.

The restriction that only one such as "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma), when qualified by an attribute that is not itself to be accomplished, can be construed as the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) is untenable; enough of this digression. // 8 //

Now, [the opponent might argue] that in the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna), there is indeed the burden of resorting to secondary indication (upalakṣaṇā) during the process of linguistic acquisition (vyutpatti); to this, he says:
"And in the case of word-meanings as well, this same [requirement] exists for the cognition of the syntactic relation through the totality of factors. (9)

Even for one who holds the view that word-meanings themselves convey their mutual connection, this must necessarily be accepted in order to establish the cognition of a specific connection: namely, that only those word-meanings possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*) convey the sentence-meaning,
and no others.
If one is questioned as to how this is so, the response should be stated as: "Because it is observed to be thus in the linguistic usage of the elders.
Therefore, since this applies equally to both positions, it does not constitute a valid refutation. // 9 //
But even so, by what distinction was abhihitānvaya abandoned and anvita-abhidhāna adopted?
However, this power of theirs is unseen; it is not understood from any other means of knowledge.
It is to be understood as being produced by contact with subsequent words that convey a specific meaning. // 10 //
For when objects are cognized through a means of knowledge other than verbal testimony, their capacity to convey mutual syntactic connection is not perceived;

therefore, one must postulate that those things denoted by words possess the power to bring about such comprehension. And regarding the arising of that power, it must be accepted that contact with the word itself is the cause.
For it is observed that in worldly transactions, a word is employed with the intent of conveying a specific meaning;
and since it is not capable of directly conveying the meaning of a sentence, it makes the meanings of the individual words its intermediate operation.
And if those [words] were capable of conveying the mutual connection [of meanings] among one another, then they would constitute intermediate operations; otherwise,
this capacity of theirs manifests only through contact with words whose purpose is the comprehension of a qualified object.
Even for a word, one must admit a capacity to instill the power to convey the mutual connection residing in the word-meanings.
This would indeed be so—if the word-meanings, which are ascertained through other means of knowledge, lacked the capacity to comprehend their mutual connection.
But that capacity does exist, as in the case of whiteness perceived by direct perception when its specific substrate has not yet been determined.

This is because we observe that there is a cognition of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*)— namely, "A white horse is running"— with respect to a horse whose specific qualities have not been apprehended, which is inferred from its visible gallop and sound, and whose footfalls are inferred from the sound of its steps; and with respect to the act of running, whose distinct agent is unknown.
"For one who sees the white form and hears the sound of neighing, as well as the sound of the hooves striking the ground, there arises the cognition: 'A white horse is running.'"
"Released from the statement in perception" (*dṛṣṭāvākyavinirmuktā*)—
this means "formless," that is, having an unmanifest form.
By this, it is meant that a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*) is not determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

To this it is replied: Is this cognition, "A white horse is running," for that very person by whom the two sounds—the sound of neighing and the sound of footsteps—were perceived as having a common substratum with whiteness;
or rather, for one who has no determination regarding the source [of those sounds]?
Regarding that [objection] as well— "What follows from this?"—
if it is said that [the fault applies] to one who brings about the defect of wandering through paths where the nature of the object has not been clearly discerned,
then there is a contradiction with experience (*apratīti-virodha*).
For he proceeds in this manner: "Surely there must be a horse in this place, and there must be someone running";
then, by virtue of the proficiency gained through practice, he perceives the sound of the horse's hooves alone as a sharp, resonant clatter.
At that time, he infers that the movement is indeed possessed of speed as it exists in the horse; he does not, however, perceive it as something isolated,
but rather understands its positive concomitance (anvaya) through the capacity of the word's meaning.

Even for one who, having ascertained that there is no other horse in that place, determines through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) the horse as the source [of the neighing], he also determines that "horseness" (the property of being a horse) resides in the same locus as the whiteness of the neighing sound.

For such a person, just as the perception of absence from the house leads to the cognition of existence outside, so too is this a case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*): "This which is white..."

The proof for this is the statement, "This is that horse. However, for one who determines that the neighing sound and the clatter of the hooves are co-located with whiteness, there is likewise an inference regarding the horse's nature and its swift movement, based precisely on the presence of whiteness.
Not [from] two independent [words].

Therefore, it is not observed anywhere—apart from inference (*anumāna*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—that word-meanings appearing as unconnected by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possess the capacity to indicate a mutual relationship.
Moreover, if the understanding of mutual connection [of meanings] were to arise merely from the comprehension of the word-meanings themselves, [then...]
In that case, it must be stated in which means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) its inclusion lies;
it cannot be in verbal testimony (śābda), because of the absence of words.
For it is your established doctrine that verbal cognition is that which arises from a word through its intermediate operation of denoting the meaning;
therefore, this [cognition] is not included within the category of the verbal.
If another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) were admitted, however, verbal testimony would be abolished,

because it would follow that even in cases concerning objects already understood through words, that other means alone would possess authority. Therefore, one must postulate a capacity in the word-meanings expressed by the words— never before observed elsewhere— to bring about the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

Since the capacity for such denotation belongs to words as well, it is more logical—on the grounds of parsimony (*kalpanālāghava*)—to postulate that words alone possess the mere power to convey their own meanings as connected (*anvita*).
By this, the view that words possess a capacity for the connected meanings only through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*) is refuted.

[Objection: But surely, one would have to postulate an infinite number of word-powers, as the objects of the words' powers would consist in the conveying of their own meanings as connected with an infinite number of counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*).
In the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the denotation of meanings followed by their syntactic connection), however, it is held that a single word has only one power with respect to a single meaning.

This is not so; for, just as in the case of the eyes and other sense organs, a single capacity—namely, the power to denote its own meaning as connected with another meaning that is expected (*ākāṅkṣita*), proximate (*sannihita*), and compatible (*yogya*)—is sufficient to account for the diversity of effects according to the difference in the counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*).
Just as the eye, through its single power of vision, produces distinct cognitions of jars and other objects due to the difference in the accompanying counter-correlatives such as the jar itself.

In the same way, it should be understood that the word [itself] also [differs] due to the difference in its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*). Furthermore, since this is equally applicable to the meanings of words (*padārtha*) as well, this [objection] amounts to nothing.
Others, however, say: "The meanings of words, when possessed of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*), become the sentence-meaning."
Nor, however, do they [the words] merely cause the sentence-meaning to be understood.

This [position] is extremely weak—because it would entail the consequence that there is no cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. If words are not the means for the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*), then even the word-meanings cannot be the cause.
It would follow that [the effect] arises without a cause.
This might be thought:
When a meaning that requires a complement has been expressed by either a verbal form or a nominal form,
whatever other word brings into proximity another suitable counter-correlative entity, [that is the basis for the relation].
"In that case, it remains as being related to that"—
this is true; however,
it must be stated what the basis for that relationship's cognition is.

Now, when the preceding word-meaning has been expressed as being expectant [of a complement], that other word which is uttered brings its own meaning forward precisely as being related to that [preceding meaning], just like a suffix (*pratyaya*).
Just as when a suffix is uttered after the meaning of the stem has already been cognized, it denotes its own meaning as qualified by that [stem], so too does another word.
As it has been said: "The stem and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together" (Mahābhāṣya).
The meaning is that the base (prakṛti) brings its own meaning forward as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya), and thus the suffix expresses that [base] meaning;
so it has been said:
“When a cognition is produced regarding a specifically qualified object,
it is because that [object] is distinguished by a previously known meaning of the base (prakṛti).”
[Objection: "In that case, you have admitted that the second word expresses its meaning as already connected [with others], yet you still claim this is not so for the first word. [Reply: No.
Because there is no fixed rule regarding the order of application for the quarters (pādas) within a sentence;
that which is sometimes first may at another time be second.
It follows that there is denotation of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) for all words whatsoever.

Furthermore, the proponent of the theory of the relation of what has been denoted (*abhihitānvayavāda*) maintains that even in the case of a verbal root and its suffix—which possess distinct powers determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—there is only the relation of what has been denoted, just as in the case of words.
And thus:

“When it is said that ‘the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together,’ this is stated thus because of their predominance, even though they denote [their respective meanings] through distinction.”
“The root *pac* itself denotes the cooking, and the suffix *aka* also denotes the agent;
however, the agent as connected with the act of cooking is not denotable by either one [of them] alone. (1143)
Thus he says:
furthermore, if the cognition (*pratyaya*) expresses the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāyin*),
then, since there is no distinction in that regard, why is it not accepted that words (*pada*) themselves also express the related meaning?
What is the use of this partial destruction?
If there is indeed denotation of the related (anvitābhidhāna) even for both the base and the suffix,
then why should the door not be opened by the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) that arises from the impossibility of denoting the related in the case of the word "dvāram"?
The word "when concealed" (*saṃvṛtāyām*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
It is said:
"the door"—this [word] is the first [example], denoting a meaning that is not distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
Therefore, what is it that is denoted here as being associated [with the verb]?

Regarding the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) in cases such as "enter" where the suffix conveys a distinct meaning, there is no fault, because— just as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others— it occurs precisely because the expressed meaning would otherwise be untenable.
Regarding the subject matter of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), the view of Bhaṭṭapāda is as follows:

However, the venerable Vārttikakāra-miśras, not accepting that all sentence-meanings are secondary (*lākṣaṇika*), reject the assumption of a capacity in word-meanings to understand their mutual connection (*anvaya*).
For a word-meaning denoted while in an unconnected state (*ananvitāvastha*) indicates its own related state of being connected (*anvitāvasthā*) through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*).
For since there is a relationship between a state and that which possesses the state,
when that which possesses the state is expressed,
the state itself necessarily becomes present to the mind.
Moreover, it is an established fact that whenever one related member of a relation is perceived,
a cognition of the other related member arises; therefore,
there is no need to postulate a separate power in words for the communication of a meaning already associated with others.
Regarding this, they say:
"It is our established position that in every case, it is indeed the sentence-meaning that is indicated.
On this point, others say: "This is not indication (lakṣaṇā)."
Because its own primary meaning is not abandoned;
for it is observed that figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs in cases such as the Ganges only through the abandonment of the primary meaning.
However, they speak thus due to a deficiency in their inclusion within the system of Mīmāṃsā.
For, depending on the requirements of what is to be characterized (*lakṣaṇīya*), there may be either the abandonment or the inclusion of its own primary meaning (*svārtha*).
In the expression "he bestows forms upon the *sṛṣṭi*s," there is the acceptance of a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Because those possessing qualities— those enumerated as such even when devoid of the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi)— are observed [to be implied], and because they are included therein, the meaning of "creation" is understood. Likewise, in the statement "he sacrifices on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsīṃ yajate*), since the singular number would otherwise be untenable, the word *paurṇamāsī* denotes the sacrifice itself for the purpose of indicating a collection of sacrifices.

Furthermore, when the aggregate is grasped, there is no abandonment of the members of that aggregate, because the latter are the substratum of the former. Similarly, in a copulative compound (*dvandva*) expressing mutual conjunction, since the dual or plural number would otherwise be untenable, a state conjoined with other referents is resorted to through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And there is no abandonment of the state [possessed by the base];
likewise, in the *Niṣādasthapati* section (*Mīmāṃsā-darśana* 6.1.10), it is said in the prima facie argument that there would be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the sense of the genitive case,
yet even there, the abandonment of the meaning of the stem (*prakṛtyartha*) does not occur.
Likewise, in the case of "with the sound of the chariot" (*rathaghoṣeṇa*), there is no abandonment of the chariot.

Similarly, the mantra ending in the singular number, "to the lord of the sacrifice, the sacrifice" (*medhapataye medham*), is applied to the archetype (*prakṛti*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*);
and there is no abandonment there of the two possessors of the quality, Agni and Soma.
Even when its own primary meaning is not abandoned, indirect indication (lakṣaṇā) is indeed appropriate.
This is the determination of indirect indication according to the opinion of the Guru (Prabhākara).
To this, it is said:
But how, then, does this indication (lakṣaṇā) function?

It is called indication because of the connection of the expressed meaning with the sentence-meaning, which is otherwise impossible; it occurs through the inclusion of that [meaning] which is brought to bear by virtue of its connection [with the primary meaning]. (1151)
This is the summary verse (1152):
"In such expressions as 'a crocodile in the Gaṅgā,' because the literal meaning of the word *gaṅgā* cannot be construed within the meaning of the sentence,"

Having abandoned that [direct denotation], it is determined that the object such as "the bank," which acquires proximity to the cognition through its connection with that [denoted meaning], possesses the status of being integrated into the sentence-meaning.
For this very reason, they say:
"By way of inconsistency..."
And it is through a relation that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs.

In this context, in such cases as “Bring the cow,” there is no incompatibility of the literal meaning with syntactic connection, because the already connected meaning cannot enter into another connection.

Now, let it not be that this is a case of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā); rather, the action, having understood its connection with the factors of action (kārakas), makes known its own state, because of their inseparable relation (avinābhāva).

It is said: first of all, the verbal nature of the comprehension of the syntactic relation has been denied in this manner; however, it is admitted that [the relation] falls within the scope of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*).
Thus, the comprehension of a specific syntactic relation, being untenable, would result in being rootless.
Now, since linguistic usage is impossible without a connection to a specific [meaning], the utterance of words would be purposeless; therefore, one must resort to such a connection.
Even so, because those who act with foresight employ only meaningful sentences, the understanding of a connection to a specific meaning arises from their speech.
However, in the case of the Veda, it should not be purposeless.

Because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not possible to understand the connection with a specific [meaning]. Nor does it follow that this would result in meaninglessness even in common worldly usage; for this reason alone, it is not logical to determine the connection with a specific [meaning] even in the absence of a means.
For indeed, the taking up of water by one who desires to burn is not considered meaningless.
The power to burn may manifest in water;
let there be a lack of purpose [in that case],
but there is no lack of determination regarding the positive concomitance of the specific instance in the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
Now, since it is understood from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) that words have as their purport other things that are desired, proximate, and capable [of being related],
the comprehension of a specific relation follows according to that [established] linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*).
Therefore, in that case, the words do not have that [specific relation] as their purport in the very usage of the elders.
Or else, how indeed could the meanings of words be established in the absence of a means?
This is our thought; for we consider that [the cognition of meaning] would otherwise be untenable without postulating a power (śakti) either in the words themselves or in the word-meanings. // 10 //
And since that [capacity] belongs only to words, he says: "It is better to accept that capacity as belonging to the words themselves. (11)
It is not proper to bypass the words that arise first and rely on the meanings for the power to convey the sentence-meaning; moreover,
it is beyond dispute that words are, at least initially, denotative.
Therefore, since their expressive power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) is already established, it is easy to assume that this very power extends as far as the syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
In contrast, for word-meanings (*padārtha*), one must assume a separate power of cognition (*bodhana-śakti*).

Therefore, following the principle that "the postulation of a property (dharma) is better than the postulation of a substratum (dharmin)— it is more parsimonious"— it is appropriate to postulate that words themselves possess the power of denoting a related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*). Furthermore, since words are accepted as being expressive,
if they were to produce a cognition of word-meanings that has only their own individual forms (*svarūpa*) as its object, [they would fail to convey the intended sense].
Even then, its status as a denoter would be lost,
because that cognition arises from the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which brings about the understanding of the object at the time when the relationship was first grasped.
Indeed, for the sake of establishing the recollection of the relationship, one must necessarily admit the awakening of the latent impression that causes the recollection of the related object.

Therefore, since the denotative capacity of words consists precisely in their acceptance as conveying a related meaning that was not already apprehended at the time of grasping the relationship [between word and object], one who accepts this must resort to the theory that words denote the related (anvitābhidhāna).
As for the one who—
“The word does not differ from the reminder because there is no additional [content].”
[Ślokavārttika, Adhikaraṇa 6, Verse 107] Thus:
"First of all, that which expresses the bhāvanā causes it to be remembered, as is the case in common worldly usage."
Since this is seen in the words of the Teacher [Ślokavārttika, Adhikaraṇa 7, Śloka 248], he states that the denotative power of words consists precisely in their being reminders;
in response to that, he says:
"Also because of the acceptance of [their] purport."
Even that proponent who maintains that words merely serve to remind one of word-meanings must nevertheless admit that words have the purpose of conveying the sentence-meaning;
otherwise, it would follow that the sentence-meaning is not derived from verbal testimony (*aśābda*).
If this is so, let the words themselves possess the power to directly convey the meaning of the sentence; what is the use of resorting to an intermediate [stage]?
Therefore, those who claim that words have a denotative function (*abhidhāyakatva*) toward word-meanings, distinct from their merely reminding one of them, [are refuted].
Regarding these, there is an assumption of three capacities:
first, the capacity of words to denote their meanings; and second, the capacity to instill the power to bring about the cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) residing in those word-meanings.
And [it is] the capacity to make known the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of word-meanings.
For those who maintain that words merely cause recollection, it is more parsimonious to abandon the capacity for denotation (*abhidhāna-śakti*) and postulate two capacities;
furthermore, by the very logic already stated, it is more appropriate to postulate the capacities in the words themselves.
It has been established that words denote [their meanings] as already connected. // 11 //
Now, in order to avoid the previously mentioned fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), he demonstrates how the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence arises from its constituent words:
All the words heard are first recalled as having meanings that are not yet syntactically connected;
subsequently, once their individual manifestations have been brought about by logical reasoning, they convey the meaning of the sentence.
One who has not grasped the relationship [between word and meaning], or for whom the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) from grasping that relationship has not arisen,
or whose impression has perished, is not qualified for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.

But one whose mental impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the apprehension of the uncorrupted relationship [between word and meaning] remains intact, upon hearing a word, necessarily remembers this: "This [word] is the designator of that [object] as connected with a counter-correlate that is required, proximate, and appropriate.
And thus, by one who remembers in this way, the very form (*svarūpa*) of the indivisible [words], though not yet connected, is indeed remembered.
No one maintains that the meaning of a sentence is understood upon hearing only a single word;

for even according to the proponents of the theory of the relation of the expressed (abhihitānvaya-vāda), as long as another word does not present another meaning, there is no comprehension of the syntactic relation.
Because a word-meaning that conveys its syntactic relation (anvaya) depends upon other word-meanings,
and because a relation itself depends upon its counter-correlate (pratiyogin),
even in that view, all words must express their own meanings as unrelated [to others].

Subsequently, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning must be admitted to arise from all those [words] once they have ascended to the level of memory. Thus say the venerable authors of the Vārttika:
"For even they do not lead us to the understanding of the sentence-meaning when they are not remembered."
Therefore, it is only when those recollections are combined that they possess the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
[The *Bṛhaṭṭīkā* says:
"For this very reason, the definition of a sentence by our venerable Teacher is: 'A sentence is words that express a meaning collectively' (*Śābarabhāṣya*, Bālamanoramā edition, Adhyāya 1, Pāda 824).
Now, one might ask: how do those who maintain the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) arrive at the comprehension of the sentence-meaning?
For how could an object that has not been cognized by a word while it is being heard appear when that word has vanished?

It is replied: even for the proponent of the theory of the connection of what is expressed (*abhihitānvayavādin*), there is no such rule that only the final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions produced by each preceding phoneme, is the conveyor of the word-meaning.

For it is observed that even from the Veda, which was studied during childhood and whose meaning was not previously ascertained, there arises an understanding of the meaning later on when it is remembered after the refinement of knowledge regarding its constituent parts (*aṅga*).
Therefore, there is no fault in [the Veda] being a means of comprehension once it has ascended to memory.

For, since the denotation of a related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) depends upon a correlative, the meaning was not denoted at first due to the absence of the necessary auxiliary factors while the word was being heard.
What is illogical about saying that [the meaning] is expressed afterwards?
Even those proponents who say this— “Let there be only one word that expresses the related meaning,
while the other words function merely to bring the correlates into proximity”— [are not refuted].
Nor is there a lack of apprehension of a distinction, because a distinction is apprehended either by virtue of being first mentioned or by virtue of being the principal term.
For this very reason, they say:
"Either the first word is the sentence, or the principal word is the sentence" (Vākyapadīya, Kāṇḍa 2, Śloka 2).
He replies to them: "Everything.
If only the first [word] were to possess the status of a sentence, then all word-meanings would have to be construed with the meaning of the first word.
Nor is there this restriction:
that because of the statement, "One purchases Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, yellow-eyed cow" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.9), redness must be connected only to the act of purchase.
Furthermore, because there is no fixed order of sequence among the words in a sentence, [the qualities may be connected to any other word].
It is not tenable that at one time that very [word] expresses [the object] as accompanied by existence (*sadanvita*), while at another time it does not;
likewise, it is also untenable for a principal word (*pradhānapada*) to possess the nature of a sentence (*vākyatva*).
Because all [the qualities] lack syntactical connection with the substance *soma*;
for although all [qualities] such as *āruṇya* (redness) possess a purpose directed toward the *soma*,

Because it is apprehended first, and because the intention (tātparya) is admitted to reside in the meaning of the sentence. // 15 //

It is on the basis of this much similarity that the illustration is given.
Not in its entirety.

Listen with attention to the entire essence of the Prābhākaras.

Therefore, since the relation (*anvaya*) is already grasped through the meaning in the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), this relation is not itself expressed.

"The sentence has that alone as its purpose.

And if this [denotation] were not accepted, [the following would occur].

In the view of those who maintain that words denote [their meanings] as already associated with a universal (*sāmānyānvitābhidhānavāda*), the words first terminate their expressive power in that alone; nor is it admitted that word-meanings possess the power to convey a mutual relation (*anvaya*).
Furthermore, even the implication of a universal does not necessarily reach a specific instance.

Therefore, even when a specific [meaning] that is desired and compatible is brought into proximity by another word, its connection would not be cognized at all due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes that connection.

However, in the view of those who maintain that there is a specific concomitance (viśeṣānvaya), those factors which entered as conditions for the apprehension of the relation are utilized in the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. // 20 //
Thus he says:
"In the theory that the relation is understood through linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), [the capacity] enters as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*);
but in the theory of the connection with particulars (*viśeṣānvayavāda*), it is helpful by way of fitness (*yogyatva*) and so forth. (21)

It has been shown previously that in the theory of the denotation of meanings as related to particulars (*viśeṣānvitābhidhāna*), factors such as semantic competency (*yogyatva*) enter as limiting conditions (*upādhi*) within the linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) that "the meaning of a word is to be understood as connected with the meanings of other words"; these are helpful in that context, but not in the theory of the denotation of meanings as related to universals (*sāmānyānvitābhidhāna*). // 21 //
He states another objection:

"Furthermore, since the connection with the universal is established by the very force of the thing itself, those who desire that [universal] to be denotable have exerted their efforts in vain regarding words. (22)
Even by examining the nature of action and its factors (*kāraka*), since the understanding of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is established through the mere factor and the mere action,
it is futile to accept that a word denotes the connection with a universal (*sāmānya*). // 22 // 1216 //
Is it the sentence as a whole that is not perceived? Or is it only the final phoneme of the sentence? Is it the collection of words residing in memory? Or is it the very first word?
Either the mere verbal form alone, or the word-meanings unconnected [with one another],
or the cognition of a general connection, is the cause for the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

"Words alone are capable of bringing about the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, provided they possess their respective parts and express the connection with specific qualifiers. These are the summary verses.
And so it has been said: "Does a word have a meaning?
"Certainly it does."
How, then, is the relationship between the sentence and its meaning innate?
It is through the linguistic usage of elders;
this is true.
It has been stated that [the meaning] consists of the parts of the *satva*.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction," of the *Vākyārthamātṛkā* with its commentary (*vṛtti*), composed by the Great Preceptor Śrīmat Śālikanātha Miśra.
Now begins the second chapter of the *Vākyārthamātṛkā* with its commentary.
The prima facie argument regarding the object of the action (kārya). Having established the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna) as an introductory premise,
and desiring to prove that the meaning of Vedic sentences is an unprecedented action (apūrva-kārya), the proponent first states the prima facie argument:

Now, regarding words that depend upon linguistic convention to express their meanings, how can it be said that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others denote a "task" (*kārya*) that is not known through any other means of valid cognition? (1)
In the section on the *apūrva* (Mīmāṃsādarśana 2.1.2), it was stated that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is the *apūrva*.
Furthermore, the *apūrva* is held to be something incapable of being apprehended by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And whatever is incapable of being apprehended by other means of valid cognition—
In that case, the apprehension of the relationship is impossible,
because it is preceded by the apprehension of the relata;
for it is by observing the linguistic usage of specific objects that the expressive power of the word regarding those objects is inferred.
And that very [cognition] is the apprehension of the relationship; furthermore, regarding that which is not cognized,
no linguistic usage concerning it can be determined.
And if that [object] is not ascertained, the cognition having that as its object cannot be inferred;
and if that cognition is not inferred, on what basis could the capacity of the word be postulated?
Furthermore, the *apūrva* is not within the scope of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
nor is it understood from the word alone without the determination of its relationship [to the result].
Because that which has its power exhausted lacks the capacity to cause comprehension;
and because the capacity is understood precisely from the fact of causing comprehension.
It might be argued:
This is the power of the word *liṅ* (the optative suffix) and others: that it conveys its own meaning even when its potency has not yet been fully determined.
For, since the derivation of *liṅ* and other suffixes from common worldly usage is possible by accepting their capacity to convey mere action (*kriyā*), [there is no need for a separate injunction].
For it is untenable to postulate that something is expressive while its relationship [to the meaning] has not been grasped, especially when it differs from other words.
If it is argued that this is postulated because the cognition of an unprecedented action (*apūrva-kārya*) arises from a Vedic sentence, we say no;
for that very [cognition] is unestablished.
[The opponent argues: "It is action (*kriyā*) itself that is understood from Vedic sentences as the object to be accomplished (*kārya*);

however, by the force of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), one perceives an *apūrva* (unprecedented) effect as the object to be accomplished—a notion that is merely a mental fabrication lacking any authoritative basis.
Therefore, how can the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, whose relationship [to the object] has not been grasped, denote an *apūrva* effect?
And thus, how can that be the meaning of the sentence?
For only that which is denoted (abhidheya) constitutes the meaning of a sentence. // 1 //
And thus—
how could other words also, by means of that unseen [relation], express their own meanings as connected [with others] in some instance, when they lie far beyond the path of linguistic usage? (2)
Since that [inherence] is not perceived, its correlate is not perceived;

and since the determination of the relationship [between word and object] is impossible therein, the capacity of other words to convey their own meanings as connected with that [inherence] is cast far aside. // 2 //
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*). He introduces the final position: "In this regard, it is said: when indeed a single elder has spoken..."
"O Caitra, bring water," [he says]; then Caitra brings the water. // 3 //
Then, another person desiring to acquire proficiency understands it thus:
"This activity of his is preceded by an intention, just like my own.

Having observed that the elder’s activity, which has a specific object as its domain, occurs immediately after hearing a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, [he concludes this].
Desiring to emerge [from the womb], the infant reflects thus: "This activity of my own, which is under my control, must be preceded by cognition, just as it was in my case.
Furthermore, this reflection arises in him: "Just as I proceeded after having cognized..."
This case is also like that: whatever object the cognition— which serves as the cause for this activity— has, while being directed toward that object, becomes the cause of my activity.
Since his activity also has that very same object, inference arises once again for one who desires to understand;
thus, these two inferences constitute the independent activity of the elder, which has as its subject (dharmin) [the aforementioned state].
"Preceded by intelligence" is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*), because it proceeds independently, like my own independent activity.

Likewise, "the intelligence that serves as the cause for the activity of an elder" is the subject (*dharmin*); the property to be proven is that the object of his intelligence is the very same as the object of the intelligence that serves as the cause for my own activity.
"Because it is a cognition that serves as the cause for my activity, like the cognition that serves as the cause for my own activity"—
thus this reflection occurs again for him,
and it is this [reflection] that is made known by the word.
By this other means of knowledge (māna) of mine, that object which is the domain of that cognition— the cause of its engagement— is made known by this word;
for it is understood when that [object] exists.
"But for me, that [object] is made known by another means of knowledge"—this is the distinction between us.

Therefore, he determines that the word's capacity to make known the object that serves as the cause for its application consists in this: that which prompts my activity once it has been understood is made known to him by this word. (3.1.2)

Furthermore, in order to determine what that object denoted by the word is which serves as the cause for engagement, one reflects upon the object established within oneself that serves as the cause for engagement:
"In that case, having understood it, did I previously engage [with it] on my own? (4)
Independent of words, one who is acting spontaneously wonders, "Having cognized what have I begun to act?

By the phrase "at another time," the state prior to linguistic mastery (*vyutpatti*) is expressed. That which was previously perceived by the child, once linguistically proficient, as the cause for his own activity—
The meaning is that it is postulated that this very [nature] belongs even to one who is proficient [in language], and nothing else; thus,
there is a rejection of the status of *bhāvanā* for both the word and its operation.
Therefore, it is refuted that the injunction (*vidhi*) is either the word itself as the cause of activity, or its operation;
for neither of these is perceived by a child as being the cause of activity within himself.
Furthermore, these two positions have not been directly introduced and refuted because they are extremely weak.
To explain: if the very form of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) were the motivator, then all who hear them would necessarily be prompted to act;
however, this is not observed to be the case.
Since activity occurs for someone at some time,
let the gods perhaps accept the reliance on the operation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth as the cause of such activity;
we humans, however, whose eyes are made of flesh, are not capable of fathoming such a domain of epistemic authority.

The presentation of the verbal *bhāvanā*. What is this verbal *bhāvanā*? It is said to be of the nature of the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, conducive to the production of a person’s activity (*puruṣapravṛtti*).
Its instrument (*karaṇa*) is its own cognition.
An impelling force (preraṇā) is postulated as being conjoined with a procedure characterized by the excellence proclaimed in the *arthavāda* passages.

For, according to the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*), all injunctive texts, as well as the Self included under the term "one's own Veda," are enjoined thus: "One should meditate upon Him" (*bhāvayet*)—so states the *Tantravārttika*, p. 114.
In that context, when there is the expectation "what [is it]?", human activity (*puruṣapravṛtti*) is connected [as the object].
When there is the expectancy "by what means?", the knowledge of the injunction (*vidhijñāna*) itself is accepted as the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of its suitability;
for it is the verbal productive urge (*śābdabhāvanā*), once known, that brings forth activity.
