By its very fitness, the knowledge of excellence arising from the *arthavāda* enters into the factor of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). For the power of the injunction (*vidhi-śakti*), which would otherwise fail, is supported by the knowledge of excellence.

And that *arthabhāvanā*—which consists of human activity, is delimited by the result such as heaven, has the meaning of the verbal root as its instrument (*karaṇa*), and possesses the assistance of the instruments produced by the ritual elements obtained through Śruti, Smṛti, and custom—is expressed by the same suffix [that expresses the apūrva].
Regarding the phrase "having become objects"—
that is the refutation of that [position].
That is not so.
There is no evidence whatsoever that such an operation exists in the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such verbal endings.

If it is argued that the very activity of a person occurring immediately after the word ending in *liṅ* and so forth constitutes the evidence, we say no; for activity is never observed elsewhere to be caused by such a [supernatural] basis.
For activity is observed to have a basis; having observed that very basis, it is possible to infer [the cause],
but not a specific operation of sound whose causal nature has never been apprehended before.
Now, the audacious claim that the word itself— such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth— is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is untenable,
because that which has not had its relationship [with its meaning] grasped cannot be expressive; for indeed, when the correlate is not determined, [the word cannot convey its sense].
Because of the absence of any cognition of a relationship [between them],
and because, in that context, all injunctive elements as well as the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*) are themselves enjoined,
and the injunction impels the person toward the objective productive activity (*arthabhāvanā*).
And whoever is impelled by something is constrained by it;
moreover, it is not possible for insentient injunctions to possess even the capacity to constrain.

Now, it might be argued that words are enjoined to impel [the person]. That too is untenable—because all words possess agency (*kartṛtva*) by their very nature with respect to verbal productive operations (*śābdabhāvanā*), they do not depend on being enjoined. Or, if it is argued that non-persons are not enjoined to impel, [then...]
But even that [injunction] is not possible for the purpose of making the meaning understood; for in that case as well,
the lack of dependence on a person to be enjoined (niyojya) remains the same.
And because it is accepted that the injunction for study, which consists of the refinement of syllables, is the very injunction for the act of studying;
as they have said:
"In what [category] among substances and so forth, then, would the Veda (svādhyāya) be included?"
In this regard, the determination of the nature of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) appears in three ways.
And in the enumeration of things to be refined, the refinement of the syllables is indeed appropriate;
for in the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya), that very [Veda] is clearly and directly refined as the ritual act itself.
Thus,
the injunction for a consecration does not enjoin the object to be consecrated,
because that which has its utility established by another means of knowledge possesses the status of being the primary purpose (the *śeṣin*).
However, a ritual injunction for a consecration (*saṃskāra-vidhi*), which culminates in the consecration itself, cannot imply an action to be performed by the object to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*).
Furthermore, it is untenable because both alternatives— that the self (*ātman*) is enjoined by the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) or that it is not enjoined— are impossible.
There is the rejection or non-rejection of the status of being something-to-be-accomplished (bhāvya) regarding human activity. And how is there human activity? What is its object to be accomplished?
It cannot be [the result] because it is produced immediately [after the activity].
Otherwise, it would follow that knowledge of the procedure lacks the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
For in that case, human activity would be the fruit of the action;
yet an action does not require an instrument for the production of its own fruit.
Furthermore, motion does not depend upon an instrument for the initiation of conjunction and disjunction.

It might be argued: "The word, such as one ending in the optative suffix (*liṅ*), having generated the cognition of an injunction, initiates its own operation in the form of an impulsion, assisted by the instruments."
Nor is there an absence of instrumentality, because instrumentality exists precisely in the accomplishment of an action;
this [notion] is indeed extraordinary.
For it is not observed that the cognition of any object whatsoever is the cause for its own production;
thus, the status of being an *itikartavyatā* (procedural requirement) is refuted for the cognition of commendation (*prāśastya*).
In this way, even for the commendation expressed by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), its status as an *itikartavyatā* is set aside from the injunction (*vidhi*).
For its existence in that manner is due to its capacity;
and it is not possible to understand its capacity to assist the cognition that serves as the instrument when the instigation—whose agent is the word—is produced.
However, there would be an understanding of its capacity in relation to an activity whose agent is a person.

Because human activity is observed toward what is commendable (praśasta). It might be thought: if human activity were impossible toward what is not commendable, then instigation itself would not be tenable.
That is incorrect;

for it is well known in the world that the accomplishment of an action does not depend upon the occurrence of its result, whereas the establishment of the result depends precisely upon the accomplishment of the action.
Therefore, even in that case where [the injunction] is fruitless, activity would occur because the impulsion (preraṇā) is established.
Now, if the fruit also is included within the section on the procedure (itikartavyatā), just like the excellence (prāśastya),...
Therefore, in its absence, no impulsion is accomplished.
Well then, let the fruit itself be that which completes the constituent part of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*); what is the use of commendation?
This is true;
since that [injunction] also exists, it should not be abandoned.
If that is so, then let there be no dependence upon it when the commendation has not been heard.

Consequently, the postulation of that extended application (*atideśa*) and so forth is untenable; even the postulation of the *karaṇa* (means) and *itikartavyatā* (procedure) for a mere injunction is nothing more than a mere postulation, like the case of the *darvihoma*. Furthermore, the example "like the *darvihoma*" is unestablished (*asiddha*), because in that case too, it is accepted that the assistance is provided solely by means of the procedure consisting of the *ācamana* (sipping of water) and other elements obtained through Vedic texts, traditional recollection (*smṛti*), and established custom.
For it is not possible for a single entity to be both the benefactor and the beneficiary within itself.
Now, if it is argued that the word indeed performs the instigation, [we reply:]...
But activity does not arise from that alone;
rather, it occurs when there is knowledge of that.
If this is so, then let activity be the very fruit of knowledge.
It is not the fruit of instigation,
because it exists when that [instigation] is present and does not exist when it is absent.
And thus it is established that verbal bhāvanā is not the injunction. Furthermore, sound is a quality of space; otherwise, for space, which has become the auditory organ, [it would not be perceived].
Furthermore, since it is impossible for sound to reach [the sense organ], and since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are the two forms of such reaching—
wherein conjunction arises either from the action of one of the two factors or from the action of both— [neither can apply here].
And since sound cannot exist with space if it were a substance produced by conjunction— and given that [substance] is restricted to being of three kinds—
it follows by the method of elimination that "attainment" (prāpti) is inherence; thus,
sound is a quality of space.
Furthermore, an operation is not possible for it [the word],
because operations reside in substances.
How, then, is an operation characterized as denotation attributed to the word?

Listen to how it is so: when that cognition of an object within the self which arises immediately after the cognition of a word is intended to be expressed as having the word as its agent, then it is called "denotative" (*ābhidhānika*).
Even when the operation resides in another, agency indeed exists, just as it does for the self in the case of motion;
thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
And how is this [action] the object of the *arthabhāvanā* (the productive operation of the meaning) which is the function of the word?
As it has been said:
"The reason why the injunction (*vidhi*) and the *bhāvanā* are grasped by a single suffix is..."
"First of all, a relation is determined from the meaning of the verbal root."
[Ślokavārttika, Adhikaraṇa 7, Śloka 79 1/2–80 1/2] Thus it is said; but that is not so.
On this view, it is difficult to maintain that the suffix expresses *bhāvanā*,

because there arises the suspicion that all verbal suffixes denote *bhāvanā*. For is it not the case that the fact that all verbal suffixes express *bhāvanā* is determined by their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb "to do" (*karoti*)?
For instance: *bhāvanā* is the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) with respect to the agent of the root-meaning;
that very thing is *kṛti* (volitional effort), because that which is being brought into being (*bhāvyamāna*) is precisely what is being done (*kriyamāṇa*).
Because it is the object of the action of making; what did he do? He cooked.
What does he do? He cooks.
Does he cook? What will he do? Will he cook?
From the observation of this question and answer,
it is understood that the meaning of "to do" (karoti) is expressed by all verbal suffixes;
otherwise, the answer would be inappropriate to a question concerning the object of the meaning of "to do."

In that regard, even though the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is present in words ending in the suffix *dhañ* and others, the meaning of "doing" is not understood; whereas, when a verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) is in proximity, that meaning is indeed understood.
Therefore, it is determined that the meaning of *sā* (the action) belongs to the verbal forms alone.
The refutation of that [position]:
That is incorrect.
If the meaning of the question "What does it do? is "That which it performs,"...
If one asks "Why is that? and the answer there were "Because he cooks," then the word *pacati* functions in the sense of "he performs cooking."

And thus it would be established that verbal roots have "acting" (*karoti*) as their meaning; yet this is not the case, for when the specific activity denoted by the root has not been understood, [the meaning of the verb remains ungrasped].
It is precisely that specific [meaning] which is thus questioned, and "he cooks" (pacati) is the answer;
and in this way, it is not established that verbal suffixes (ākhyāta) express a meaning of "doing" (karoti) distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha).

And all verbal roots (dhātvartha), by conforming to the coming-into-being of something previously non-existent, attain the sense of "doing" (karoti) and thus can be questioned and specified by means of the verb "to do"; therefore, they are [the objects of] questions and answers regarding their specificities.

Furthermore, since the question and answer are logically consistent even on the basis that they refer to a specific operation denoted by the verbal root itself, it cannot be asserted that verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) express a meaning of "doing" (*karoti*) distinct from that.
Moreover, in the case of Devadatta and others who perform actions involving effort, the distinction between operations is possible; therefore, the question and answer would be appropriate.

If the object of the question "What does he do? were a distinct sense of the action of doing (*karoti*), then the answer "He goes" would be logically untenable, because there is no activity distinct from going. However, if the scope of the question is the specific meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), then it is indeed tenable even in that case.
Now, even in that case, if conjunction and disjunction are the meaning of the verbal root (dhātu) and motion (parispanda) is the meaning of the suffix (vibhakti),
there is still no inconsistency, because an operation distinct from the meaning of the verbal root is possible therein as well.
That is not so;
for it is only motion (*parispanda*) that is denoted by the root *gam*.
To explain: [the meaning of the verb] is not merely conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Alternatively, the root *gam* (to go) is used in the sense of separation,
because it is not employed when a hawk is either joined with or separated from a post.
Nor can it be both, for that would entail the application [of the term "goes"] even to a post when a hawk has flown up and landed upon it.
If it were argued that the conjunction and disjunction produced by a single moment of action are what are denoted by the verb "to go," [we reply:]...
In that case, let action alone be the denoted meaning; why is it included within the category of adventitious attributes (*upādhi*)?
For in this way, the burden of relying upon adventitious attributes is indeed avoided.
Moreover, the determination of word-meaning is derived from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).
Now, there is no inconsistency in the usage of elders that cannot be accounted for unless verbal roots denote *bhāvanā*.
As for the question and answer, however, they occur subsequent to the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning].
Therefore, the determination of the relationship [between the verb and its object] cannot be based on that [the agent];
since the use of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is justified by its denoting merely the number of the agent and so forth, it is not possible to postulate any further denotable meaning.

Moreover, in the sentence "Devadatta performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti devadattaḥ*), the word *pāka* expresses the meaning of the root *pac*, while the verb *karoti* denotes the human effort corresponding to that [action],
and the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) expresses only the number of the agent.
Thus, its denotation of the mere action is established;
therefore, it is logical that it applies to other cases as well in that very same way.
Likewise, the analysis of "Devadatta cooks" (pacati devadattaḥ) is: "he performs cooking" (pākaṃ karoti).
That too is untenable;

for in the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*), it is possible to provide an explanation by taking up with the root *kṛ* (as the base) that human effort which, through its connection, renders the meaning of *paci* something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Even in cases where there is no further effort [expressed] such as "the chariot performs going," one should understand that the use of the verb "to do" (*karoti*) is figurative, intended to show that going is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Because [the argument] is equal in both cases,
[we proceed to] present and refute the opinion of Maṇḍanamiśra.

As for the one who asserts that verbal roots have "exertion" (*prayatna*) as their meaning— on the grounds that in the linguistic usage of elders, such as in the sentence "Devadatta cooks rice," the term is used for exertion which is distinct from the meaning of the root-base (*prakṛti*).
He should be instructed as follows:
"My child, do you not know that 'the meaning of a word is not obtainable through any other means'?
And here, since the effort required for comprehension is justified even by the implication of the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*),"
It is not possible to maintain that verbal suffixes (ākhyāta) denote that [action];
rather, it is only those denoting an effect (*kārya*) that are established as denoting effort (*kṛti*).
Now, do not the Prābhākaras also maintain that the verbal suffix denotes *bhāvanā*?
It is said: we do not accept that all verbal suffixes denote *bhāvanā*;

rather, the optative (*liṅ*) and other such suffixes, which express what is to be done (*kārya*), are held to denote effort (*kṛti*), because the "to-be-done" cannot otherwise be expressed. For the "to-be-done" is necessarily connected with effort; indeed, it would not be expressed if effort were not expressed.
For it is not possible that there is an act of creation which is not denoted, while the effect itself is denoted.
Now, it might be thought: just as in the case of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), the staff is not denoted by the suffix,
and yet there is a cognition of a person qualified by that [staff].
The same would apply here as well; that is not so,
because even there, the staff is not perceived.
There is no cognition [of the object] in that which possesses it;
yet the word "staff," which serves as the base form (prakṛti), exists there, and it is that which causes the cognition of it.
And this is not possible here,
because there is no fixed rule that the *prakṛtis* denote the activity of the person (*puruṣa*).
For the conscious person understands the task through the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth.
And since that [agent] is not himself capable of understanding the action as being connected with the performance by another, it must be admitted that there is an expression of his own performance;
and his performance consists in the form of effort (*prayatna*).
Nor is it the case that, because there is no experience of that [object] in every respect, those [words] are denotative of it;
thus, this is not the domain of the "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) maxim.
It might be thought:
Just as the verbal suffix (liṅ) expresses only the number of the agent and so forth, while the agent and others are understood through the implication of the action,
so too here the action implies effort.
"Let it not be that [the effort] is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*)"—
this is incorrect;
for although the effort is implied by the action which constitutes the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*).
Nevertheless, how is the *apūrva* understood through its dependence on that [effort]?
When effort is denoted, that which is perceived as delimited by it is understood to have its accomplishment dependent upon it, and not otherwise.
Nor is the *apūrva*, when denoted merely by its own nature unqualified by an action (*kṛti*), capable of implying that effort.
For it is an entity whose relationship [to an action] has been understood that is implied;
and there is no cause for understanding the relationship of an unprecedented (*apūrva*) thing with effort except through a word.
Therefore, how could it imply that effort?
Therefore, those who maintain that [the Vedic word] denotes an unprecedented effect (*apūrva*) must necessarily resort to the expression of "effort" (*prayatna*);
this has been demonstrated more skillfully in the *Viṣayakaraṇīya*, so let us refrain from further prolixity. // 4 //
In this regard, I have not engaged [in action] merely by understanding the action alone, nor merely the result,
nor merely the connection between the action and the result.
Even when there is an understanding of the relationship between the action and its fruit as that of the means and the end, activity does not occur;
for one does not engage in eating when the cause of satisfaction has already passed,
nor when it is currently present.
Even if that [result] were to occur through its accomplishment, it would be like what is described by those who know the marks of the ocean; for there is an absence of actual performance.

Furthermore, while the comprehension of a person's intention might be suspected as a cause for engagement, it is cast far aside in the case of independent activity for one who desires to learn [the meaning].
However, having recognized something as an action, I have engaged in it; perceiving "this is my duty," I am everywhere engaged.
For instance:
Let alone worldly activities such as going and coming;
even at the very least, there is the activity of drinking mother’s milk and so forth, which brings about satisfaction. (5)
As long as it was not determined that "this is my duty," I never at any time engaged in it. // 6 //
A doubt arises according to the view of the *Brahmasiddhi*.
Here, another says:
"It is true—that activity proceeds only from the comprehension of an effect."
But "taskness" (kāryatā) is simply the state of being a means to achieve what is desired; it is nothing else.
That very [state], which is the cause of engagement, is called an injunction (vidhi).
Thus he says:
"The wise maintain that an injunction is simply the state of being a required means;
for it is from this [injunction] that determination and so forth arise, neither spontaneously nor from mere verbal expression."
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya Vārttika, Kāṇḍa 3, vv. 103½–104½, p.
115] Thus:
"For a person, there is no other motivator toward actions than the fact that they are the means to a desired end."
They declare that the dharma which is the cause of engagement is "pravartanā" (the act of setting in motion).
[VI. vi. Śloka 26, p. 243] Thus:

"For it is the worldly understanding that 'what is to be done' (kartavya) is a means to what is desired by the agent; however, in the opposite case, it is 'not to be done' (akartavya) with respect to that object."
And so it is said [in verse 30, page 302].
This is its refutation.
In that regard, first of all, this very point must be stated:
The fact that the past and the present possess the status of being a means to a desired end does not mean they are determined as "to-be-done" (kārya) in that sense;
therefore, "to-be-done-ness" is something else.
"Any other [notion of] being a means to a desired end"—

thus, since activity also does not depend on the mere cognition of that [desire], he sets that aside for now and points out the distinction between being a means to a fruit and being a task (kāryatā).
That which is called "being a means to a result" is not at all "being an effect.
For "being an effect" consists in being achievable through volitional effort (*kṛti*), whereas "being a means to a result," on the other hand, [consists in something else]. (7)
The state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) with respect to the production of a result differs between the two;
even though both are directed toward a single object,
there is nevertheless a difference in their essential natures (*svarūpa*).

For that very same entity is called the "means of accomplishing the result" (phalasādhana) because it serves as the means toward the result, and it is called the "task" (kārya) because its own acquisition of being depends upon the action to be performed. // 7 //
To the question, "Why is it that the understanding of what ought to be done applies only to the means for attaining the desired, and not elsewhere? he says:
"But rather, an action that is itself of the nature of suffering proceeds toward the status of being something to be done. (8)
In that case, the state of being a means to a result is the cause, and by that, there is the state of being an effect;
since it always arises from the existence of that [cause], it is that very [state] which is manifested at that time.
For actions are by their very nature causes for the arising of suffering;
the understanding of them as effects is based on the understanding of them as means to a result.
Indeed, being an effect does not consist merely in having its accomplishment dependent upon an agent.
However, that which is primary with respect to the act of creation and whose existence is dependent upon it is called the "effect" (kārya);
and that [effect] is the primary object of the act of creation.
That with reference to which an action proceeds [is its object];
yet it is not tenable that an action proceeds with reference to suffering or the cause of suffering,
nor with reference to what is not suffering.
Nor as a cause of suffering;
rather, as happiness or a cause of happiness.
In that regard, action is not itself of the nature of pleasure; furthermore, if it were not even a means to pleasure,
the understanding of its primacy with respect to purposeful activity would not be possible.

Therefore, the understanding that ritual acts (*karman*) are to be performed is based on the understanding that they are means to a result; thus, being a means to a result— which falls within the category of indicators (*jñāpaka*)— is dependent upon the state of being a task (*kāryatā*),
yet it is not identical in essence to that state.
And thus, even pleasure that is not a means possesses the nature of being an effect;
for everyone understands pleasure as an effect, and does not depend upon its being a means to another fruit.

Having determined, "My activity proceeds from the understanding that [the act] possesses a *kāryatā* (state of being what is to be done) transcending its status as a mere means to a result," and seeing Caitra engaged in activity, the learner infers: "Caitra also acts because of the cognition of a *kārya*. In this inference, Caitra’s activity is the subject (*dharmin*).
"Preceded by the cognition of an effect"—this is the property to be proven (sādhya).
[The reason is: "because it is an activity while being preceded by an intellect," just like my own activity.
Furthermore, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, which denote objects that serve as causes for activity, denote the effect itself.
Because that very thing which has been understood is the cause immediately preceding purposeful activity. // 9 //
Although desire is the cause of activity,
it is nevertheless not denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like;
for its comprehension is not required for activity to occur.
For that [cognition] which has arisen is the cause of activity, not [the cognition] as it is understood.
To the question, "Even so, how is there an understanding of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others in the sense of a task (*kārya*)," he says:
"Just as other words are indeed understood in their own respective meanings..."
Likewise, in the case of an action, the optative and other suffixes function through the distinction of insertion (āvāpa) and deletion (dvāpa). // 10 // 1260 //
Upon hearing a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) or similar, one infers the cognition of a specific task through the resulting activity that arises from it,
and thereby determines the causality of the sentence. Even in that case, when investigating which meaning is expressed by which word, [one proceeds as follows].

Since the comprehension of the object to be accomplished (kārya) is observed when the optative suffix (liṅ) and others are present, and is not observed when they are excluded, it is established that the optative suffix and so forth possess the expressive power (vācakatva) for the object to be accomplished, just like other words; for it is these very elements that produce the comprehension of the object to be accomplished. // 10 //

Now, one might object: "Since verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) are learned through worldly usage as denotators, they ought to be understood as denotators only of commands (*praiṣa*) and the like, because it is only there that their employment is observed. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For it is precisely the task (*kārya*) that is superior, equal, or inferior for speakers..."
Due to the distinction based on the person being prompted, it receives designations such as "command" (praiṣa) and so forth. // 11 //
An action being communicated by a superior speaker with respect to a person who is to be prompted is designated as *praiṣa* (an injunction);
[when communicated] by an equal,
it is *adhyeṣaṇā* (a request).
Regarding the request by one who is inferior:
even the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others, which convey commands and the like, express only what is to be done (*kārya*), not some other object. // 11 //
How, then, is it determined that it is the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) alone that receives the designations such as *praiṣa* (command) and so forth? To this he says:
"For in all cases of activity, the *kārya* alone is the single cause.
Because it is invariably concomitant with activity, it is determined to be the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the like. (Verse 12)

For an activity initiated by a child is understood to be preceded by the child's own comprehension of something to be done; and seeing all persons engaged in activity, the child assumes that their engagement is likewise based solely on the comprehension of something to be done; thus, even the activity prompted by commands and the like is grounded in the comprehension of something to be done.
It is established that it is the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) alone that is associated with designations such as "command" (*praiṣa*) and the like.

However, in reality, since commands and so forth are invariably concomitant with activity (*pravṛtti*), and since the *kārya* is the cause of all activities, it is determined that even in the case of commands and the like, the meaning of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others is indeed the *kārya*. 12.
By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), moreover, does a fool understand his own task, from which he proceeds? To this, he says:
"That which is to be accomplished through effort (*kṛti*) and is primary is designated as the 'task' (*kārya*). (Verse 1268)
And that [cognition] is also to be known by another means of valid cognition, like the cooking of rice.

Since [the action] exists when there is volitional effort (*kṛti*) and does not exist when it is absent, its status as being achievable through volitional effort is first understood through inference; that is,
that toward which volitional effort proceeds.
The primary factor is volitional effort (*kṛti*), and effort is exertion (*prayatna*);
and that [exertion] is known through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
The fact that an effort has a specific purpose is also directly perceivable.
Therefore, the effect is understood through both perception and inference,
as in the case of the act of commanding and the act of cooking.
Nothing is untenable here.
He concludes:
"In this way, the optative and other suffixes are understood even in the case of an object that consists of an effect."
Likewise, other words as well [function] in their own meanings when accompanied by that [suffix]. (14)
Even so, raising the objection as to how the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others can denote an effect that is not cognizable through other means of knowledge,
he introduces the Mīmāṃsā inquiry: "In this regard, it must be deliberated here whether that effect is of the nature of an action."
Or rather, that which is distinct from that... //
Regarding what the final determination is in this matter, he says:
"In that regard, [it is] according to worldly convention. (15)
Although it may be argued that action (kriyā) is an effect (kārya) cognizable by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara),...

For in the world, since one observes the performance of a specific action upon hearing a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) or the like, it is logical that the optative suffixes and so forth produce an understanding of an object as something to be done (*kārya*),
because the understanding and the subsequent activity share the same object.
Indeed, it is not the case that [one acts] after having understood something else as the thing to be done.
Otherwise, the fool would proceed [to postulate something else].

Furthermore, if it is accepted that an action—which is the result (*kārya*) and is conveyed by a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth—is indeed [the meaning], then there would certainly be parsimony in the postulation of a capacity (*śakti*).
For instance, let the verbal root itself express its own meaning.
However, it is accepted that the optative (liṅ) and other suffixes occur after a verbal root that expresses an object as it actually exists [in the future].

Upon hearing the optative and other such suffixes, one understands that the verbal root has been employed with the intent of referring to such an existing object; thus, the comprehension of the meaning of the verbal root—which constitutes the "thing to be done" (kārya)—is accomplished.
Just as there is the determination of the present time and so forth from the *laṭ* and other suffixes,
the meaning of the rule (*sūtra*) regarding those [suffixes] is simply that the *laṭ* occurs after a verbal root when the action is in the present;
the only thing expressed by the *liṅ* and other suffixes, just as it is for the *laṭ* and others, is the mere number of the agent and so forth.
Even if those incapable of discrimination understand that action alone is what is to be accomplished according to the Veda,
nevertheless, the sixth [chapter] and subsequent siddhāntas remain established in the Veda. // 16 //
It is established that those desiring heaven and so forth are intended as the persons to be enjoined (niyojya) regarding the task;
thus, they must be expressed by words such as "one who desires heaven. (17)

For this was stated at the beginning of the sixth [chapter]: "It is beyond dispute that when an optative suffix (*liṅ*) or similar term is employed, there is an understanding of a task (*kārya*) to be accomplished;
and a task is something to be achieved through volitional effort (*kṛti*).
Its acquisition of its own nature occurs only when there is an agent."
And the acquisition of an agent occurs only when there is an understanding of an action related to oneself, not otherwise.

Therefore, although according to worldly convention the meaning of a sentence consists of the action alone— since it is understood as the thing to be accomplished (kārya)— the meanings of the other words are also [included] because they are connected with that [action].

Since no other [factor] besides being an agent (*kāraka*) can possibly be connected with the action, it is understood that the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is construed as a qualification of the agent, with the purpose of conveying the desire for heaven as a qualifier according to the maxim of the "red turban" (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*).
Nevertheless, the construal must be described as occurring solely by virtue of being the cognizer of the task related to oneself.
It is precisely the status of being that which presents the person to be enjoined (niyojya) that is accepted—thus [ends the commentary on verse 17].
To the question "Even so, what [follows]? he says:
"And there is a task for the person to be enjoined, which he perceives as his own.
To the further question "Even so, what [follows]? he says:
And because it is conjoined with desire, heaven and so forth are understood solely as that which is to be accomplished. // 18 //
For in all cases, desire is directed only toward that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*);
therefore, by virtue of its connection with that [desire], heaven and so forth—which constitute the object to be accomplished—qualify the person as something desired.
Thus, [the person] is qualified by a specific desire for heaven and so forth, extending up to their status as objects to be accomplished.
Only that [means] would be able to bring about the effect which is the means for achieving what is desired.
The presentation of Maṇḍanamiśra’s view:
Here someone says— although it is understood that heaven and so forth are things to be accomplished (sādhya) due to their connection with desire, nevertheless,
the understanding that they are the objects to be accomplished by the action under discussion is entirely without proof.
For even that which is to be accomplished by another may itself be something to be accomplished;
nor is there necessarily a means for whatever is desired.
For one whose mind is captivated by a succession of desires, there is nothing that does not become an object of longing;
yet, it is not possible to accomplish all of that.
Some also desire omniscience,
yet there is no possibility of a means for it;
moreover, for one who desires that [omniscience], agency in what does not accomplish it is not tenable.
How could this not be possible? For we observe that even those desiring to go to a village engage in spontaneous actions.
Moreover, every person indeed seeks prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
Nevertheless, it is observed that one generally engages only with those sensory objects that are contrary to that [liberation].
To refute this, it is said here: for one who desires heaven and the like, only that [heaven, etc. can be understood as the object to be accomplished (*kārya*).

Only that which is conducive to the accomplishment of what is desired [is understood as the task]; otherwise, while one is desiring it, that [means] would not be cognized as something to be accomplished. For one who has not abandoned the connection with the desire for that [result] cognizes its means as something to be accomplished.

Therefore, when something is taught as a task for one who desires a particular result, it is understood—precisely through the impossibility of its connection with the duty of the person prompted—that it is the means (*sādhana*) for that desired end. // 19 //
If this is so, what is the result? He says:

"If the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth were to signify an effect (*kārya*) as being nothing other than an action (*kriyā*), then the connection with the person to be impelled (*niyojya*) would be lost at that very moment. (20)
He asks "How so? and replies:
For an action, due to its momentariness, is not capable of producing heaven and the like—which are desired as results occurring at a later time. (21)

Furthermore, that [action], which does not produce the desired object and is subject to momentary destruction, cannot be connected as something "to be done" with the person to be enjoined who seeks a result. (22)
That action is the opposite of its effect is established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For motion (*parispanda*), which culminates in conjunction with a subsequent location, is quickly perishable;
whereas heaven (*svarga*) is to be enjoyed in a specific other place and at another time.
A restatement of Maṇḍanamiśra’s view:

[Objection] But was it not established in the first section of the sixth book that heaven (*svarga*) is a term denoting mere pleasure (*prīti*), because the word "heaven" is applied to substances that serve as the means for attaining pleasure?
Furthermore, their usage is not based solely on their own intrinsic nature,
because that [usage] would cease once pleasure has vanished;
nor is it tenable for them to be words expressing the means to that [pleasure] if they do not denote it.
If one accepts that [the word] denotes that [object], then it is simply its denotative capacity;
for the application [of the word] is justified by establishing it through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), since there is no need to postulate a primary denotative power (śakti) in that case.

Furthermore, because the word is indivisible, the logic of the "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) cannot apply; for it is only the constituent word "staff" (daṇḍa) within that whole which can convey the meaning of a staff.
Moreover, it is simply impossible for pleasure to arise immediately after an action.
This is its refutation.
It is said:
The use of the word "svarga" (heaven) in injunctions such as the Jyotiṣṭoma cannot be understood as denoting mere pleasure,
because in the explanatory passages (arthavādas), it is heard that it is a pleasure brought about by longing, to be enjoyed for a very long time and unmixed with suffering.

In that case, if the word "heaven" (*svarga*) occurring in the injunctive statement were not explained as referring to such pleasure, then the function of the words in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), which are otherwise extremely remote [from the injunction], would not be respected; therefore,
it is determined that the word "heaven" is employed precisely with reference to that kind of pleasure in order to accord with them.
And being of such a nature, it must necessarily be experienced in another place;
therefore, it does not arise immediately after the action,
and thus the causal efficiency of an action that perishes very rapidly cannot be conceived in that regard.
For it is a worldly convention that when something is produced by that which precedes it, the latter is the means (*sādhana*) for the former;
therefore, those who claim that even a perished action is understood by the scripture to be a means [to the result] are [refuting this].
These [arguments] are also refuted.

Furthermore, such an action, being destroyed so rapidly, cannot be connected as something to be accomplished (*kārya*) with the person enjoined who desires heaven, because it is impossible for it to serve as a means (*sādhana*) toward heaven. // 20–22 //

Therefore, that which is capable of being connected with the person to be impelled (niyojya) is declared by those words expressing an injunction to be the "task" (kārya)—something that persists until another time and is distinct from the [momentary] action (kriyā). // 23 //
Now, let it be that action alone is denoted as the "thing to be done" (kārya); let that very action be the means for accomplishing the fruit.
Consequently, its connection with the person to be impelled (niyojya) is indeed possible.
But how can that [action], being momentary in its destruction, serve as the means for attaining heaven, which is to be experienced in another body?
It is said in reply:
rather than that, it is better to postulate its persistence for a very long duration on the grounds that [its momentary nature] would otherwise be untenable.
Furthermore, there is no postulation of an unseen or unheard object that exceeds those [two].
Or rather, let it be accepted that the power of the action itself is enduring;
yet neither of these two deserves to be postulated, because they contradict other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For that which is non-contradictory can be postulated for the sake of establishing what is perceived;
however, the long-term persistence of an action that perishes very quickly is contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[This concludes] the presentation and refutation of the Vārtika view.
Furthermore, since it is established by another means of valid cognition that when the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) has passed away, the power (*śakti*) itself has also passed away,
it is not possible to postulate that this [power] is enduring. Moreover, once the substratum (*āśraya*) has ceased to exist, [the power cannot remain].
Upon what basis does this power abide? If you say it abides in the self, [we reply:
a power belonging to one thing does not reside in another.

Precisely because of contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, if the capacity (*śakti*) were non-existent, it would not be logical for there to be a fruit (*phala*) of that capacity.
For the means of accomplishment is that which possesses power; power alone is not [the means], otherwise it would not possess the nature of being a power.

The doubt that the grace of the deity is the cause of the fruit [of action], verse 1293: Now, it may be argued that ritual acts such as sacrifice, being means for propitiating the deity, may indeed be designated as the "action" (kārya); for through its proximity to that deity, it is certainly capable of producing the fruit even at a later time.
The deity, who is capable of bestowing the fruit, is propitiated by means of ritual acts.
"She, when propitiated, becomes gracious;
and being gracious, she certainly endows the performers with the fruit even at a later time"—
this is what is being refuted.
This is not so;
for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that sacrifices and the like are causes for propitiating a deity.
Indeed, there is no proof whatsoever that sacrifice is a means for propitiating a deity.

But surely it is remembered that sacrifice (*yajña*) is intended solely for the purpose of worshipping the gods; and all worship is understood to have the purpose of propitiating the one being worshipped.
It is said:
memory is not a means of valid cognition, precisely because it is memory.
Furthermore, the description of the meaning of the Smṛtis depends upon other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
because they follow after them;
and it has already been stated that by no other means of valid cognition is it understood that a non-sacrifice (ayāga) is a means for accomplishing a deity.
Therefore, sacrifice (*yāga*) is the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity;
it should be understood that its nature as "worship of the deity" is figurative (*gauṇa*),
for even worship proceeds only by being directed toward that which is to be worshipped.
Furthermore, that [divinity] which is the object of propitiation is itself propitiated by ritual acts;
and it is understood that the deity is the recipient of worship consisting of sacrifices performed by a person traveling to various locations.
That which possesses a body is indeed contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in its capacity as an object of cognition;
furthermore, the Veda’s presentation of such a being as an object of worship from time immemorial is likewise contradicted by other means of knowledge,
because it is impossible for that [embodied being] to be beginningless.
Furthermore, since this matter has been refuted at length in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (Mīmāṃsādarśana 9.1.4),
one need not exert much effort here; namely,
the suspicion that sacrifice serves as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person.
Now, it might be argued that the action, which serves as the cause for the refinement of the person, is denoted by the word as something to be performed;
and since that action is connected to a person such as one desiring heaven, the fruit will arise at a later time precisely from the refinement of the person.
That is not so.
This is because there is no evidence for the view that [rites] serve to purify the person;

for neither through other means of valid cognition nor through verbal testimony is it determined that sacrifices and the like are causes for the purification of the person, as stated in the passage: "Rites [are for the sake of the sacrifice], because they are to be accomplished by being commenced," etc. (Mīmāṃsādarśana 11.1.20).
The suspicion that it is the action that is the object to be accomplished:
"But surely, let it be the action itself that is said to be the object to be accomplished,
and let its status as the means to the fruit be accepted as belonging to that very [action]."

However, since that [direct denotation] is otherwise inexplicable, let some other thing be postulated as its effect—conducive to the arising of the result, persisting over time, and residing in the self—so that it need not be the denotation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.
This concludes the exposition of our own position: that the "task" (*kārya*) is what is denoted by the optative suffix and the like.
It is said: for that [auxiliary] is postulated because of the impossibility of that [primary action] otherwise, provided it is that which makes the primary action possible.
However, the status of the action as a means to the result is not thereby established by some other imagined factor produced by the action that generates the result.
For neither the means of achieving that means, nor an intermediate operation, nor a power brings about its status as a means.

Since the status of being a means belongs to those things possessing power precisely through their connection with an operation, and since neither an intermediate operation nor a power inherent in the self constitutes an additional entity for actions, it is not logical that such an operation should be cognizable through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

However, since the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of related meanings) is established, it is well said that, because of its conformity with the person to be impelled (*niyojya*), it is precisely as a verbal meaning that [the object] is desired;

thus: "Even a task (*kārya*) that persists until another time, which is capable of being connected with the person to be impelled and is distinct from the action itself, is expressed by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth alone."
A description of the entire essence of the Guru’s doctrine (gurumata).
1297. Herein is the method:
in the *Codanāsūtra*, it was established that [the Veda] has action as its purpose.

In the first section of the sixth book, it was established that the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) and so forth is the *niyojya* (the one to be enjoined), who is to be understood as being related to that very same task (*kārya*).
Furthermore, in the first section of the eleventh book (*Mīmāṃsā-darśana* 11.1.1), it was established that the desire for heaven is a qualification of the *niyojya*.
And in the *Bādari-adhikaraṇa* (3.1.3), it was concluded that this task (*kārya*) is the cause for the production of the desired object which serves as the qualification of the *niyojya*.
And such an effect, being of the nature of an action (*kriyā*), does not exist, because it is impossible for it to be a means of accomplishing a result.
To begin with, the status of being a means of accomplishing a result by way of propitiating a deity does not exist; this has been established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* [Mīmāṃsādarśana 9.1.4].
That [the apūrva] does not exist by way of being a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person has been stated in the section on the commencement of actions (*karmāṇyārambhabhāvyatvāt*);
furthermore, that action or its capacity is not something enduring has been established in the *Apūrvādhikaraṇa* (Mīmāṃsādarśana 2.1.2).

Therefore, it is established through multiple lines of reasoning that the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. denote a task (*kārya*) inherent in the self, which is not known through other means of knowledge, by way of its connection with the person to be impelled (*niyojya*).

And the "task" (kārya) is that which is to be accomplished by human effort (kṛti); and this effort is nothing other than the exertion of persons. Furthermore, such effort does not exist without an objective base consisting of a verbal root-meaning (bhāvārtha).

It is established in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* (2.1.1) that it is precisely that which is connected [to the result] which is expressed; and it is determined in the *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa* (Mīmāṃsādarśana 2.2.1) that when that *bhāvārtha* (the meaning of the verbal root) is connected [to the result], it delimits it.
Furthermore, it was stated in the Bādari-adhikaraṇa itself that the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha), being the object [of the injunction], becomes the instrument;
and it was also stated in that very same place that the person possesses sovereignty over the meaning of the verbal root for the sake of accomplishing its own purpose. // 23 //
He states the suitability of an effect that persists over time for connection with the person to be enjoined:

"For that [effect], by virtue of its duration until another time, is capable of accomplishing heaven and so forth; thus, its connection with the person to be enjoined who desires [those results] is also logically possible. (24)

Now, as for the Commentator— who states that "the effort is the meaning of the suffix" and who holds that there is no effect distinct from action and so forth— he says the following in response to such a person:

That effect which is distinct from action and so forth cannot be known by other means of knowledge; therefore, because it is not previously established by other means of knowledge, it is celebrated as "the unprecedented" (apūrva). // 25 //
Regarding the etymological definition of *niyoga*:

[an objection is raised]—"Even if this were so, the meaning of the sentence would still be the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), not the *niyoga*; and that the *niyoga* is the meaning of the sentence is merely the prattle of the Prābhākaras. To this, he says:
That which impels the person to be enjoined by means of [the object's] being a task is designated as *niyoga* (an injunction) by those proficient in Mīmāṃsā. (26)

Even so, he explains how it can be the meaning of a sentence: "Because the task (kārya) alone is primary, its status as the sentence-meaning is appropriate; for it is that very [task] which the sentence first expresses, conjoined with the person to be impelled (niyojya) and the object. (27)
For it has been stated: "That which is presented as the primary subject is the meaning of the sentence"—
and the effect (kārya) is indeed stated as the primary subject.

The statement that "the meaning of the sentence belongs to that [liṅ-ending word] alone" is said to be generally true in the case of the expression of what is connected with the person to be enjoined (niyojya). Furthermore, the expression of what is connected with the person to be enjoined is itself generally true.

This is because [the Vivaraṇakāra] accepts the denotation of the injunctions (niyoga) that produce the primary acts— the subsidiary acts of fire-installation (ādhāna) and Vedic study— as being devoid of a person to be enjoined (niyojya).

Indeed, the Vivaraṇakāra maintains that even with respect to the subject matter of fire-installation there is a distinct injunction, since there is no recognition of the same injunction as that pertaining to the sacrifice (kratu).
For if that [substance] were not present, the recognition of the injunction would not be possible.
Nor can there be a recognition by way of fire, which—unlike the *paṇa* and so forth—is invariably connected to the sacrifice;
for in the case of the *juhū* and other implements, since their words denote the generic form (*ākṛti*), the possibility of recognizing the injunction exists even prior to the actual rule.
But surely, since the fires (*agni*) are also to be accomplished, how can two things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) be connected within a single sentence?
It is said in reply: even here, the mandate (*niyoga*) alone is the primary thing to be accomplished.
The fires possess the status of being objects that are not intended [as goals].

Even though they are objects that are not intended, because the result produced by the act of consecration (*ādhāna*) inheres in the fire, the terms *āhavanīya* and so forth are applied to it due to its connection with that result.

Furthermore, since the Āhavanīya and other fires are useful for the sacrifice (*kratu*), it is sufficient that human activity is established for the sake of accomplishing them; thus, there is no need for the expression of [an injunction] connected to a person to be directed (*niyojya*).

Likewise, it is established that even in the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), because performance is obtained through the impulsion of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*), the expression is devoid of a person to be directed.

Even the primary originative injunctions (*pradhāna-utpatti-niyoga*) achieve their fulfillment only through the performance of their own objects as implied by the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-niyoga*).
In that case, there is no search for an expression associated with a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
Regarding the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, there is no introduction of a separate injunction (*niyoga*);

for even the injunctions for the origination of the subsidiaries are established as being subservient to the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-niyoga*), since they have as their object the *prayāja* and other rites already employed [in the primary ritual].
What is the use of the theory of "denotation of the qualified" (*anvitābhidhāna*) regarding them?
But how is it that the injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth have as their object that which has already been enjoined?

It is said: when the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are heard in proximity to a primary injunction (*adhikāra-niyoga*), they are not capable of conveying a separate injunction (*niyoga-antara*) regarding their own specific objects.
Because it is possible for them to be merely reiterative, as in the case of [the words] *avadhātādi*;
rather, they present the mere essential form (*svarūpamātra*) as qualified by its own word-meaning (*svapadārtha*), which is capable [of syntactic connection].
And that [essential form], being in need of a purpose, is construed with the *niyoga* (injunction) which possesses an authoritative scope and serves as the purpose.
The optative suffix (*liṅ*) occurring within the injunctive statement itself denotes its own meaning as connected with that [apūrva].
This connection is termed "the grasping by the grasper" (*grāhakagrahaṇa*), which consists merely in the subordination (*aidamarthya*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.
Furthermore, for the apūrva, which stands in need of assistance from the instrument (*karaṇa*), there is the conceptualization of an instrumental assistance.
That is the function of the context.
In that regard, the conceptualization of those [causes] as producing assistance for the instrument is based on their material cause (aupādānika).
In this regard, there is the removal of doubt:
"Is it then not the case that there is no separate *niyoga* (obligatory injunction) in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth?

No, it is not that there is none; because those [acts] being momentary cannot logically function as a collective contribution toward the performance [of the rite], one must necessarily resort to a separate *niyoga*.

That very optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, which was previously suspected of having a merely reiterative meaning, now expresses a distinct injunction (*niyoga*). For this very reason, it is not accepted that these words such as *yajati* (he sacrifices), when occurring within subsidiary sentences, denote their own meanings as already connected to the primary injunctive mandate, as is the case with [the repetition of] threshing and the like.

That being so, at the very moment of origination (*utpatti*), since the essential nature of the subsidiary sacrifice (*aṅgayāga*) is not distinct from [the primary], it cannot be the object of another injunction (*niyoga*); thus, it would not have the status of being an object of another injunction.
However, at the stage of origination, because it is denoted as something not distinct [from the primary], its status as the object of another injunction is logical.
Why, then, is another [injunction] regarding a horizontal [sacrifice] not the object of a different injunction?
For it is impossible to understand a single entity as being simultaneously connected to two effects.
And that other injunction which exists in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—
Therefore, when that [result] is subsequently mentioned, it is denoted by its own word solely as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the application (*niyoga*) of the qualification (*adhikāra*);
otherwise, there would be a contradiction regarding the assignment (*viniyoga*) of two distinct objects. Enough of this digression. // 27 //
The refutation of the doubt regarding the subordinate status of the *niyoga*:
Now, since it is admitted that the *niyoga* is a means for attaining the desired fruit, the *niyoga*—
like the fruit itself— should possess primacy.

Since it is logical that this very [kārya] constitutes the meaning of the sentence, he says: "In order to establish the agent who is directed toward action, which is conducive to the proof of the Self, even heaven and so forth, being subordinate, are for us merely the *kārya* (the thing to be done). (28)
Since that unprecedented task (kārya) cannot be established as a task without its connection to a person to be enjoined (niyojya),
and since that [connection] is impossible without performance (anuṣṭhāna).
Because that [agency] is untenable without an agent,
and because an agent cannot exist without a qualification for action (*adhikāra*), and because that [qualification] is impossible without being subject to an injunction (*niyojyatva*).
And because there is no understanding of an injunction for one who desires [a result] when that result cannot be accomplished by his own will;
rather, the injunction, for the sake of establishing the self itself, assumes the role of being the cause for the accomplishment of the desired fruit, like a master.
Just as a master, while acting for his own benefit, renders service to a slave born in the house.
Likewise, the injunction also belongs to the person to be enjoined;
thus, there is no loss of its primary status. // 28 //
Now, since the mandate (niyoga) is the means to the fruit, and since that [mandate] is established by means of a performance consisting of the instrument together with its procedure (itikartavyatā),
the fruit would be accomplished immediately after the completion of the mandate through its performance.

Immediately following this, [the author] states the following regarding how that [result] could be established when the activity has already passed, since an injunction (niyoga) is not accomplished [at that time]: "When the object has been performed, the injunction is indeed not the result."
At that very moment, it acts in dependence upon auxiliary causes. // 29 //

This is the established position here: the injunctions for the production of the primary [rite] and the injunctions for the production of the subsidiaries are accomplished simply by the performance of their own respective objects, joined with the subsidiaries that provide assistance through direct application (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*).
Among those, as for the subsidiary *apūrvas* (unseen potencies),...
These [subsidiary apūrvas] assist in the production of the primary apūrva, and from that, the supreme apūrva is accomplished;
this also applies to the subsidiary apūrvas of the consecration rites (dīkṣaṇīyā) and so forth.
For those [subsidiaries] as well, there is one *utpattyapūrva* (origination-apūrva) arising from the subsidiaries extended by way of remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*),
and another *aṅgāpūrva* (subsidiary-apūrva), which is to be understood as being like the primary [sacrifice]. In this manner, everything else should also be inferred accordingly.

Thus, although the fulfillment of the mandate occurs immediately after the performance of the ritual action, nevertheless, the fact that the fruit does not arise immediately is accounted for by logical reasoning. // 29 //
If this were so, would not the status of the *apūrva* as a cause of the fruit be sublated? To this he says:
"The dependence on auxiliary factors does not sublate causality; lest it be sublated, one must assume its assistance in every case. (30)
The meaning is "so it is.
Therefore, the teachers [state]: "Both human effort and destiny are the means for accomplishing the fruit."
*Daiva* (fate) is *apūrva*;
it is that which must be awaited as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) for human effort (*puruṣakāra*) to bear fruit.
[This section contains] the refutation of the doubt regarding the non-mention of injunctions (*niyoga*) in relation to obligatory rites (*nitya*) and the like.

But surely, let it be so that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others denote an unprecedented effect (*apūrvakārya*) in the case of optional rites; however, how is this to be understood regarding the sections on obligatory, occasional, and prohibitory duties?
For the Prābhākaras do not admit the arising of a fruit in those cases.
For the fruit is not connected as a fruit [in itself], but rather as a qualification of the qualified person (adhikārin); however,
once the qualification of the person— such as "living"— has been obtained, [the connection follows].
What is the use of searching for a result? Nor is it impossible to engage in activity without a result, because engagement depends solely upon the comprehension of a task related to oneself.
Even though there is an understanding of the effect related to itself from a word that is independent [of external action] even without a result,
it is because only that much is understood in the world to be the cause for engagement.
It has been stated that the result (phala) is employed for the purpose of producing the cognition of what is to be done (kārya).

Now, an objection is raised: just as there is a cognition of what is to be done from the word, so too, because of the absence of a result, there would be a cognition of its not being something to be done through inference.
How is the occurrence of engagement established? It is not [established] otherwise; for if someone does not engage with a result that is merely imagined, then what is to be done? // 30 //

But surely, if the arising of a fruit is not admitted, then because the previously mentioned path would be impossible, the designation of the *apūrva* as the effect in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth would be without authority; to this, he says:
"Thus, [the apūrva] arises from a thorough consideration of the meaning of the sections concerning desires (*kāma*)."
Mastery is the basis for the comprehension of the meaning of all sentences.
It has been stated that it is illogical for a word to have multiple meanings;
therefore, once it is established that in the context of optional rites (*kāmya*) the word denotes an unseen result (*apūrva*),
that same meaning is adopted even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and the like, since there is no contradiction.

However, because the designation of [the sacrifice] as something to be performed through action is inconsistent with the permanent entitlement (*nityādhikāra*), it is untenable in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*);
thus, in all cases, the meaning of the sentence is simply the *apūrva*. // 31 //
In this regard, the following must first be stated: it is not only through worldly usage (*lokavyavahāra*) that the meaning of words is determined in the Veda;

rather, once it is established that a word expresses a meaning capable of being construed with other word-meanings due to its connection with a well-known referent, its capacity to express a corresponding meaning is indeed ascertained.

And this has been established in the *Yavavarāha-ādhikaraṇa* [Mīmāṃsādarśana 1.3.5]: since the determination of the relationship [between a word and its meaning] occurs solely through usage (*vyavahāra*), the comprehension of the meaning of other words occurs in both ways; therefore, by considering the suitability for connection with the remainder of the Vedic sentence, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that [the term *yava*] refers only to long-bearded barley and so forth.
The same applies to the word *trivṛt*.
Furthermore, because the capacity [of words] is ascertained in the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the *āhavanīya* fire, and so forth;
and because this linguistic usage is also frequently observed in common worldly practice,

it is not unreasonable to determine that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others denote the "unprecedented task" (*apūrva-kārya*), given their fitness for connection with the person enjoined (*niyojya*) in Vedic injunctions.

And this is another distinction: that while the fact that sentences containing optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth have an injunctive purpose (*kāryārthatva*) is established from the usage of elders alone, however, as for the "task" (*kārya*) which is the denotation of the optative suffixes themselves—
And that it is a form never before seen is understood solely from its connection with Vedic words—thus [ends the commentary on verse 31]. 1331.

Now, he introduces and refutes the view of a certain school: "Others, however, say that the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) is established solely through worldly usage (*vyavahāra*), with respect to an effect (*kārya*) that is not known by other means of knowledge and which is distinct from action (*kriyā*) and the like. (32)

The meaning of this is as follows: some say that because we observe activity upon hearing a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) or similar forms, and because such activity is invariably based on the cognition of something to be done (*kārya*),
the meaning of these [suffixes] is the mere "to-be-done" (*kāryamātra*) itself, not the action (*kriyā*).
The determination of the expressive power (*śakti*) of Vedic injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like resides in the "task" (*kārya*).
Now, one might object: "In this way, it would follow that linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) must be established through the Veda alone. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"This linguistic proficiency regarding the meaning of the 'task' follows from worldly usage (*vyavahāra*)."
But here, determination alone arises from the investigation of Vedic statements.
Because a word would be useless for its application in that [state],
it is determined solely through worldly linguistic usage (*laukikavyavahāra*) that a word denotes an action as a distinct effect— thus [ends verse 33].

He declares this to be improper: "But this position, like something other than white, does not attract the mind; it has been defiled by the departure from the stainless path of logic, like moonlight obscured by clouds. (34)

To the question "How so?", he says: How could a bystander, regarding an effect that is not known through other means of cognition, understand beforehand from a word the linguistic usage based upon it? (35)
Without understanding conventional usage, how can the comprehension that is based upon it and possesses its characteristics be known? And how much more so the power of words? (26)
The intended meaning here is as follows:

although it is true that only the effect (*kārya*) in general is conducive to activity and therefore constitutes the meaning of a word, nevertheless, since in common worldly usage it is observed that only when that [effect] is connected with an action (*kriyā*) does it possess the power to incite activity, [the word's meaning must be understood in that context].
It is possible to understand that [the word] is dependent upon action;
just as even when the meaning of a word is held to be the universal (ākṛti) alone, its dependence upon the individual (vyakti) is not rejected,
so too its dependence upon action, being established by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), does not deserve to be rejected.
Therefore, it is unproven that [the word] denotes an effect distinct from the action. At most, there would be a conventional usage based on that [effect];
in that case, by observing that [usage], and because the cognition which is its cause would otherwise be impossible, one might determine through inference that the word possesses denotative power.
But this is not the case;
because that [object] is not understood prior to the word, there is no comprehension of the linguistic usage based upon it.
And since that [usage] is not comprehended, there is no inference of the cognition that serves as its cause; thus, the postulation of a capacity (śakti) is untenable. // 34–36 //
In this regard, he clarifies the underlying intention: "Let it be inferred that activity is preceded merely by the cognition of an effect;
however, according to worldly experience, it is determined that the effect is indeed an action. (37)

Furthermore, since the nature of being an action as it is commonly recognized in the world cannot be denied, it is determined that when the meaning is simply "something to be done," the action itself is what is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth as the object to be accomplished; it is not, however, some "unseen potency" (*apūrva*) established through another means of valid cognition. // 37 //
The refutation of the doubt regarding the status of action as the object to be accomplished (*kārya*) according to another view:

Others, however, say that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth are understood to denote a supersensible object to be accomplished (*atīndriya-kārya*), because we observe activity proceeding from the injunctions of teachers who communicate the meaning of the Vedas.
If, even from the words of a teacher, it is only action that is understood as the object to be accomplished, [then...]

In that case, since the action itself consists of suffering, it would be impossible for one to engage in it without being connected to some other human goal; consequently, there could be no engagement by one who invariably seeks happiness. Furthermore, there is no human goal in rites such as the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*).
Therefore, it is understood from the words of the Teacher that there must be an effect distinct from the mere action.
He replies to them:
"Even in the case of engagement with the meaning of the Vedas and the words of teachers, this very same method for fully understanding the relationship [between word and meaning] must apply. (38)

Even regarding the engagement of disciples in the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other rites due to hearing the words of their teacher, a child would postulate that the very understanding of the action as something to be performed— defined by its own object— is the cause;
and since that [understanding] is untenable without a result, he would also conceive of an understanding of a result.

Even one who understands the meaning of the Veda by following worldly linguistic conventions would, in the cases of obligatory, occasional, and prohibitory injunctions, postulate a fruit [for the action]. Or rather, that same person, having become proficient during his childhood and subsequently ascending to the status of a teacher,
when teaching the meaning of the Veda to his pupils, would present the ritual action itself as that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*).
No new effect is produced—thus [it is said]. // 39 //
He summarizes:
"Therefore, the acquisition of linguistic proficiency occurs only regarding the causal aspect in accordance with worldly usage;
however, its novel nature is established in accordance with the Vedic sentences. (39)
Thus, having established that [the word "kārya"] denotes an action not previously known, he raises an objection:
"But even in this position, contradiction with common worldly usage is observed; for in the world, action is in every way understood as nothing other than something to be done (kārya). (40)
He refutes [this objection]:

"This might be so; however, even with respect to the unmanifest (apūrva) of the body, the worldly understanding and application would be contradicted if they had as their object the state of being the effect of an action. (41)

If the worldly understanding and application regarding the objectivity of action and its result were contradicted by the acceptance of our position that [the word] denotes the effect of the unseen force (*apūrva*),
then our position would be in conflict with the world; however, this is not the case, as he says:
For that which is to be accomplished through action is the *apūrva* (the unprecedented), and once it has been accomplished, the action becomes the means (*sādhana*).
Indeed, people in the world intend to express by means of words that which is cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the application [of Vedic injunctions] is consistent with the definition [of an injunction] only when the effect is an action (*kriyā*).
For the application of practice does not necessarily follow the primary (śrauta) mode of signification,
since it is observed in common usage even through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
Therefore, although by the aforementioned reasoning the "novel" (apūrva) task is indeed the denotation of the optative suffixes (liṅ) and so forth,

Nevertheless, because that [cognition] is invariably connected with being an effect of an action (*kriyākāryatva*), there is no inconsistency in applying [the terms "action" and "effect"] to those two through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
As for the objection that in common usage the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are not employed when the word-meaning itself is the object to be accomplished:

This is because that apūrva, being of a nature not previously known, is not apprehended by any other means of valid cognition, whereas worldly usage has as its object that which is already known; furthermore,
the apūrva is something to be accomplished through action.

And since an action, once accomplished, becomes a means (*sādhana*), its status as the effect of the action is eternally connected with the *apūrva*; thus, it is possible to define that [apūrva] by means of it. // 42–43 //
If this is indeed figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), why then does the world not understand it? To this he says:
"But there is no recognition of the figurative indication because of the failure to determine the primary meaning."
But for those who are skilled in the primary meaning, there arises the cognition that [the word] is figurative. (44)
Without knowing the primary meaning, people regard even a figurative meaning as if it were directly expressed by the word, just as barbarians do with words such as *yava* and *varāha*.
However, for investigators who discern the primary meaning, there arises the cognition that it is merely figurative. Thus ends [verse] 44.
He concludes:
"Therefore, the Vedic sentence declares that the effect is not known through other means of knowledge and is connected with another entity; this is the summary that has been set forth. (45)
He states the title of the work, the name of the author, and the purpose:
This *Vākyārthamātṛkā* was composed by Śālikanātha, following the doctrine of his teacher Prabhākara, for the purpose of instructing those who are free from envy. 46. 1349.
This commentary on the *Vākyārthamātṛkā* was composed by Śālīka himself, desiring to bestow favor upon those of virtuous conduct.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Vākyārthamātṛkā* with its commentary, composed by the Great Professor (Mahāmahopādhyāya) Śrīmacchālikanāthamiśra.
And thus concludes the eleventh treatise, named the *Vākyārthamātṛkā*, within the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*.
